q.t: Which of the following documents have to be on board for an international flight?
o: Certificate of registration, Certificate of airworthiness, Airworthiness review certificate, Airplane logbook, Appropriate papers for every crew member
EASA Form-1, crew papers, technical logbook
Certificate of airworthiness, ARC, EASA Form-1, airplane logbook, crew papers, technical logbook
Certificate of registration, Certificate of airworthiness, Airplane logbook, Technical logbook
q.e: ICAO Annex 6 requires the following documents on board for international flights: Certificate of Registration, Certificate of Airworthiness, Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC), Airplane Logbook, and appropriate papers (licenses) for every crew member. EASA Form-1 is a maintenance release document, not a flight document.

q.t: Which area could be crossed with certain restrictions?
q.e: A Restricted Area (R) may be crossed subject to certain conditions or restrictions as published. Prohibited Areas (P) may not be entered at all, while Dangerous Areas (D) are only advisory. 'No-fly zone' is not a standard ICAO airspace classification.

q.t: Where can the type of restriction for a restricted airspace be found?
q.e: The Aeronautical Information Publication (AIP) contains permanent information about airspace restrictions including the type, limits, and conditions of restricted areas. NOTAMs are used for temporary changes, while the chart shows the area boundaries but not full restriction details.

q.t: What is the status of the rules and procedures created by the EASA? (e.g. Part-SFCL, Part-MED)
o: They have the same status as ICAO Annexes
They are not legally binding, they only serve as a guide
They are part of the EU regulation and legally binding to all EU member states
Only after a ratification by individual EU member states they are legally binding
q.e: EASA regulations (such as Part-FCL, Part-MED, Part-SFCL) are EU regulations with direct legal effect in all EU member states. They do not require national ratification. ICAO Annexes, by contrast, are standards that states aim to implement but can file differences.

q.t: Which validity does the 'Certificate of Airworthiness' have?
q.e: The Certificate of Airworthiness (CofA) has unlimited validity as long as the aircraft is maintained in accordance with approved maintenance programmes and the Airworthiness Review Certificate (ARC) is kept valid. The ARC itself must be renewed annually.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation 'ARC'?
q.e: ARC stands for Airworthiness Review Certificate. It confirms that an aircraft has been reviewed and found to comply with applicable airworthiness requirements. It must be renewed every 12 months.

q.t: The 'Certificate of Airworthiness' is issued by the state...
o: of the residence of the owner.
in which the aircraft is registered.
in which the airworthiness review is done.
in which the aircraft is constructed.
q.e: The Certificate of Airworthiness is issued by the state of registry — the country in which the aircraft is registered. This is in accordance with ICAO Annex 8 (Airworthiness of Aircraft).

q.t: A pilot license issued in accordance with ICAO Annex 1 is valid in...
o: the country where the license was acquired.
the country where the license was issued.
those countries that have accepted this license on application.
q.e: An ICAO Annex 1-compliant license is not automatically valid in all ICAO states. It is valid in those countries that have accepted it — which typically means the license holder must apply for validation or conversion to operate in another state's airspace.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation 'SERA'?
o: Standard European Routes of the Air
Standardized European Rules of the Air
q.e: SERA stands for Standardised European Rules of the Air. It is Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 923/2012, which harmonises the rules of the air across all EU member states, largely based on ICAO standards.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation 'TRA'?
q.e: TRA stands for Temporary Reserved Airspace. It is airspace reserved temporarily for specific use (e.g., military operations) and is activated only when needed. Outside activation times, it is available for normal traffic.

q.t: What has to be considered when entering an RMZ?
o: To obtain a clearance to enter this area
The transponder has to be switched on Mode C and squawk 7000
To permanently monitor the radio and if possible to establish radio contact
To obtain a clearance from the local aviation authority
q.e: An RMZ (Radio Mandatory Zone) requires pilots to continuously monitor the designated radio frequency and, where possible, establish two-way radio contact before entry. Unlike a CTR, no ATC clearance is required, but radio capability is mandatory.

q.t: What is the meaning of an area marked as 'TMZ'?
q.e: TMZ stands for Transponder Mandatory Zone. Aircraft operating in a TMZ must be equipped with and operate an SSR transponder (typically Mode C or S) to allow ATC to identify traffic. This enhances situational awareness in busy or sensitive airspace.

q.t: A flight is called a 'visual flight', if the...
o: flight is conducted in visual meteorological conditions.
visibility in flight is more than 8 km.
flight is conducted under visual flight rules.
visibility in flight is more than 5 km.
q.e: A visual flight is one conducted under Visual Flight Rules (VFR). VMC describes the meteorological conditions, but the defining factor for calling a flight 'visual' is that it is flown under VFR, following the applicable rules for visual flight.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation 'VMC'?
q.e: VMC stands for Visual Meteorological Conditions. These are weather conditions that meet minimum requirements for visibility and cloud separation, allowing flight under Visual Flight Rules (VFR). The specific minima depend on airspace class and altitude.

q.t: Which distances to clouds have to be maintained during a VFR flight in airspaces C, D and E?
q.e: In airspace classes C, D, and E, VFR aircraft must remain 1500 m horizontally and 1000 ft (300 m) vertically from cloud. This separation is required to allow see-and-avoid and to prevent inadvertent IMC entry.

q.t: The minimum flight visibility at 5000 ft MSL in airspace B for VFR flights is...
q.e: In airspace class B (controlled airspace), VFR flights at or above 3000 ft AMSL / 1000 ft AGL require a minimum flight visibility of 8 km above FL100, and 5 km below FL100. At 5000 ft MSL (below FL100), the minimum is 5000 m.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace 'E' for an aircraft operating under VFR at FL75?
q.e: FL75 is above 3000 ft AMSL and above 1000 ft AGL. In airspace E at these altitudes, VFR requires a minimum flight visibility of 5000 m (5 km) and cloud clearance of 1500 m horizontally / 1000 ft vertically.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace 'C' for an aircraft operating under VFR at FL110?
q.e: FL110 is at and above FL100. At or above FL100, in any airspace class, VFR requires a minimum flight visibility of 8000 m (8 km). This is the standard ICAO/SERA requirement for high-altitude VFR.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace 'C' for an aircraft operating under VFR at FL125?
q.e: FL125 is above FL100. At and above FL100, in all airspace classes, SERA requires a minimum flight visibility of 8000 m for VFR operations. This ensures adequate visual range at higher altitudes where speeds are typically greater.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace 'C' below FL 100 for an aircraft operating under VFR?
q.e: In controlled airspace (class C, D, E) below FL100, and above 3000 ft AMSL / 1000 ft AGL, the minimum VFR flight visibility is 5 km. Below 3000 ft / 1000 ft AGL the minimum reduces to 5 km as well in class C/D/E, with cloud clearance requirements maintained.

q.t: What is the minimum flight visibility in airspace 'C' at and above FL 100 for an aircraft operating under VFR?
q.e: At and above FL100, the minimum VFR flight visibility is 8 km in all airspace classes. This higher minimum reflects the greater closure speeds and reduced reaction times at higher altitudes.

q.t: The term 'ceiling' is defined as the...
o: height of the base of the highest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 20000 ft.
height of the base of the lowest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 10000 ft.
altitude of the base of the lowest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 20000 ft.
height of the base of the lowest layer of clouds covering more than half of the sky below 20000 ft.
q.e: Ceiling is defined as the height above ground or water of the base of the lowest cloud layer that covers more than half (BKN = 5/8 or more) of the sky, and is below 20000 ft. It is measured as a height (AGL), not altitude (MSL).

q.t: The altimeter is switched from local QNH to 1013.25 hPa...
o: when climbing above the transition altitude.
q.e: When climbing through the transition altitude (defined in the AIP for each country/region), pilots switch their altimeter from local QNH to the standard pressure setting of 1013.25 hPa. Above this level, flight levels are used instead of altitudes.

q.t: During a flight at FL 80, the altimeter setting has to be...
q.e: Flight Levels (FL) are defined with reference to the standard pressure datum of 1013.25 hPa. When flying at a FL (above the transition altitude), the altimeter must be set to 1013.25 hPa so that all aircraft use the same reference, ensuring vertical separation.

q.t: What is the purpose of the semi-circular rule?
o: To avoid collisions by suspending turning manoeuvres
To fly without a filed flight plan in prescribed zones published in the AIP
To avoid collisions by reducing the probability of opposing traffic at the same altitude
To allow safe climbing or descending in a holding pattern
q.e: The semi-circular rule assigns specific cruising levels based on magnetic track: odd thousands (+ 500 ft for VFR) for tracks 000-179°, and even thousands (+ 500 ft for VFR) for tracks 180-359°. This ensures opposing traffic is at different altitudes, greatly reducing collision risk.

q.t: Which of the following options are possible SSR-Transponder modes?
q.e: SSR (Secondary Surveillance Radar) transponders operate in Mode A (4-digit identity code), Mode C (pressure altitude), and Mode S (selective address, extended data squitter). Mode B and other letters are not standard SSR modes.

q.t: A transponder with the ability to send the current pressure level is a...
q.e: Mode C transponders automatically encode and transmit the aircraft's pressure altitude to ATC radar systems. Mode S also transmits altitude plus additional data. Mode A only transmits a 4-digit identity squawk without altitude information.

q.t: Which transponder code indicates a loss of radio communication?
q.e: Squawk 7600 indicates radio failure (loss of communication). 7700 is the emergency code, 7500 indicates unlawful interference (hijacking), and 7000 is the VFR conspicuity code used in uncontrolled airspace.

q.t: Which transponder code should be set during a radio failure without any request?
q.e: Code 7600 is the standard transponder code for radio failure. It alerts ATC to the communication loss so appropriate procedures can be initiated. This code must be selected immediately upon realising radio communication has been lost.

q.t: Which transponder code has to be set unrequested during an emergency?
q.e: Squawk 7700 is the emergency code. It must be set immediately when a pilot declares an emergency (MAYDAY), alerting all ATC radars in range. 7500 is for hijacking, 7600 for radio failure, and 7000 is the VFR conspicuity code.

q.t: Which air traffic services can be expected within an FIR (flight information region)?
o: FIS (flight information service) and ALR (alerting service)
ATC (air traffic control) and FIS (flight information service)
AIS (aeronautical information service) and SAR (search and rescue)
ATC (air traffic control) and AIS (aeronautical information service)
q.e: Within an FIR, ICAO Annex 11 mandates the provision of Flight Information Service (FIS) and Alerting Service (ALR). ATC is only provided within specific controlled portions of the FIR (CTAs, CTRs, etc.), not across the entire FIR.

q.t: A pilot can contact FIS (flight information service)...
q.e: FIS is provided by radio communication. Pilots contact the FIS unit on designated radio frequencies to receive weather information, NOTAMs, traffic information, and other safety-related information during flight.

q.t: Which of the following options states a correct position report?
q.e: A standard position report includes: aircraft callsign, position (over or at a reporting point), and altitude/flight level. 'DEABC, N, 2500 ft' correctly follows this format. The other options contain errors in format or units.

q.t: What is the meaning of the abbreviation 'AIREP'?
q.e: AIREP stands for Aircraft Report. It is a standardised pilot report (PIREP) containing meteorological observations and other information made during flight and transmitted to ground stations for weather forecasting and ATC purposes.

q.t: What information is provided in the general part (GEN) of the AIP?
o: Warnings for aviation, ATS airspaces and routes, restricted and dangerous airspaces
Map icons, list of radio nav aids, time for sunrise and sunset, airport fees, air traffic control fees
Table of content, classification of airfields with corresponding maps, approach charts, taxi charts, restricted and dangerous airspaces
Access restrictions for airfields, passenger controls, requirements for pilots, license samples and validity periods
q.e: The GEN (General) section of the AIP contains general information: national regulations, access restrictions for aerodromes, requirements for pilots and operators, license validity, customs/health requirements, and similar administrative information.

q.t: Which are the different parts of the Aeronautical Information Publication (AIP)?
q.e: The AIP is divided into three main parts: GEN (General), ENR (En Route), and AD (Aerodromes). These are the standard ICAO-defined sections. GEN covers general info, ENR covers airspace and routes, and AD covers aerodrome-specific information.

q.t: What information is provided in the part 'AD' of the AIP?
o: Access restrictions for airfields, passenger controls, requirements for pilots, license samples and validity periods
Table of content, classification of airfields with corresponding maps, approach charts, taxi charts
Warnings for aviation, ATS airspaces and routes, restricted and dangerous airspaces.
Map icons, list of radio nav aids, time for sunrise and sunset, airport fees, air traffic control fees
q.e: The AD (Aerodromes) section of the AIP contains detailed information about individual aerodromes: classification, runway details, instrument approach charts, taxi charts, services available, operating hours, and communication frequencies.

q.t: The shown NOTAM is valid until: A1024/13 A) LOWW B) 1305211200 C) 1305211400
q.e: In NOTAM format, the C) field gives the end time. '1305211400' reads as: year 13 (2013), month 05 (May), day 21, time 1400 UTC. Therefore the NOTAM is valid until 21 May 2013 at 1400 UTC.

q.t: The term 'aerodrome elevation' is defined as...
o: the highest point of the landing area.
the average value of the height of the manoeuvring area.
the highest point of the apron.
the lowest point of the landing area.
q.e: Aerodrome elevation is defined as the elevation of the highest point of the landing area (ICAO Annex 14). This ensures pilots have the highest relevant elevation reference when setting QNH and planning approaches.

q.t: The term 'runway' is defined as a...
o: rectangular area on a land or water aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft.
rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of helicopters.
round area on an aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft.
rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft.
q.e: A runway is defined (ICAO Annex 14) as a rectangular area on a land aerodrome prepared for the landing and take-off of aircraft. It is specifically for land aerodromes and for fixed-wing aircraft, not helicopters (which use helidecks/FATOs).

q.t: What is the meaning of a steady green light signal at a controlled aerodrome directed to an aircraft in flight?
o: Return for landing, followed by steady green at the appropriate time
Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
q.e: At a controlled aerodrome, a steady green light signal directed at an aircraft in flight means 'Cleared to land.' This is part of the standard light signal code used when radio communication is not available.

q.t: What is the purpose of the signal square at an aerodrome?
o: It is a specially marked area to pick up or drop towing objects
It is an illuminated area on which search and rescue and fire fighting vehicles are placed
It contains special symbols to indicate the conditions at the aerodrome visually to over-flying aircraft
Aircraft taxi to this square to get light signals for taxi and take-off clearance
q.e: The signal square (or signal area) at an aerodrome contains symbols and signals visible from the air to indicate aerodrome conditions — such as landing direction, whether gliding is in progress, or whether the aerodrome is closed. It is typically located near the control tower.

q.t: An aerodrome beacon (ABN) is a...
o: rotating beacon installed at an airport or aerodrome to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the ground.
rotating beacon installed at the beginning of the final approach to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the air.
fixed beacon installed at an airport or aerodrome to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the air.
rotating beacon installed at an airport or aerodrome to indicate its location to aircraft pilots from the air.
q.e: An Aerodrome Beacon (ABN) is a rotating light beacon installed at an aerodrome to help pilots locate it from the air, especially at night or in reduced visibility. It rotates continuously to be visible from all directions.

q.t: What is the meaning of this sign at an aerodrome? (ALW-011 - cross/plus shape)
o: Landing prohibited for a longer period
After take-off and before landing all turns have to be made to the right
q.e: The signal shown (a cross/plus shape — ALW-011) in the signal square indicates that glider flying is in progress at the aerodrome. This warns pilots to be vigilant for gliders in the circuit which may not have radio or may be unpowered.

q.t: Who provides search and rescue service?
q.e: Search and Rescue (SAR) services are provided by both military and civil organisations, often working together. ICAO Annex 12 specifies that states shall establish SAR services, and in practice these involve coordination between civilian and military assets.

q.t: With respect to aircraft accident and incident investigation, what are the three categories regarding aircraft occurrences?
q.e: ICAO Annex 13 and EU Regulation 996/2010 define three categories of aircraft occurrences: Incident (less serious, safety implications), Serious Incident (significant risk of becoming an accident), and Accident (injury/death or substantial aircraft damage occurs).

q.t: What is the primary purpose of an aircraft accident investigation?
o: To Determine the guilty party and draw legal consequences
To identify the reasons and work out safety recommendations
To clarify questions of liability within the meaning of compensation for passengers
To work for the public prosecutor and help to follow-up flight accidents
q.e: The primary and sole purpose of aircraft accident investigation (per ICAO Annex 13 and EU Regulation 996/2010) is to identify causes and contributing factors and issue safety recommendations to prevent recurrence. It is explicitly NOT about legal blame or liability.

q.t: QFE is the...
o: altitude above the reference pressure level 1013.25 hPa.
barometric pressure adjusted to sea level, using the international standard atmosphere (ISA).
barometric pressure at a reference datum, typically the runway threshold of an airfield.
q.e: QFE represents the atmospheric pressure at airfield elevation. When set on the altimeter, it reads zero on the ground.

q.t: Which is the purpose of the altimeter subscale?
o: To reference the altimeter reading to a predetermined level such as mean sea level, aerodrome level or pressure level 1013.25 hPa
To adjust the altimeter reading for non-standard temperature
To set the reference level for the altitude decoder of the transponder
To correct the altimeter reading for system errors
q.e: The subscale allows the pilot to set the reference pressure (QNH, QFE, or standard 1013.25 hPa) so the altimeter displays the correct altitude/height.

q.t: In which way may an altimeter subscale which is set to an incorrect QNH lead to an incorrect altimeter reading?
o: If the subscale is set to a higher than actual pressure, the indication is too low.
If the subscale is set to a lower than actual pressure, the indication is too high.
If the subscale is set to a lower than actual pressure, the indication is too low.
If the subscale is set to a higher than actual pressure, the indication is too high.
q.e: A higher pressure setting on the subscale mechanically increases the indicated altitude. This is dangerous because the aircraft is actually lower than indicated.

q.t: Lower-than-standard temperature may lead to...
o: an altitude indication which is too high.
a correct altitude indication as long as the altimeter subscale is set to correct for non-standard temperature.
an altitude indication which is too low.
a blockage of the Pitot tube by ice, freezing the altimeter indication to its present value.
q.e: In colder-than-standard air, the air is denser and pressure drops more rapidly with altitude. Thus, true altitude is lower than indicated altitude (the altimeter over-reads).

q.t: A flight level is a...
q.e: Flight Levels are pressure altitudes expressed in hundreds of feet, based on the standard reference pressure of 1013.25 hPa.

q.t: A true altitude is...
o: a height above ground level corrected for non-standard pressure.
an altitude above mean sea level corrected for non-standard temperature.
a height above ground level corrected for non-standard temperature.
a pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature.
q.e: True altitude is the actual vertical distance above Mean Sea Level (MSL), which requires correcting the indicated altitude (with QNH set) for non-standard temperature deviations.

q.t: During a flight in colder-than-ISA air the indicated altitude is...
q.e: Cold air is denser, meaning pressure decreases faster with height. The altimeter will register a higher altitude than the aircraft is actually flying (indicated is higher than true).

q.t: During a flight in an air mass with a temperature equal to ISA and the QNH set correctly, the indicated altitude is...
q.e: If the atmosphere perfectly matches the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) and the correct local QNH is set, indicated altitude exactly equals true altitude.

q.t: Which instrument can be affected by the hysteresis error?
q.e: Hysteresis is a lag in the aneroid capsule's response within the altimeter, often noticeable after rapid altitude changes (e.g., steep descents).

q.t: The measurement of altitude is based on the change of the...
q.e: Altimeters work by measuring the ambient static air pressure, which predictably decreases as altitude increases.

q.t: Which of the following options states the working principle of a vertical speed indicator?
o: Measuring the present static air pressure and comparing it to the static air pressure inside a reservoir
Static air pressure is measured and compared against a vacuum
Measuring the vertical acceleration through the displacement of a gimbal-mounted mass
Total air pressure is measured and compared to static pressure
q.e: The VSI measures the rate of change in static pressure by comparing the immediate static pressure entering the capsule against the delayed static pressure in the instrument case (reservoir).

q.t: The vertical speed indicator measures the difference of pressure between...
o: the present dynamic pressure and the dynamic pressure of a previous moment.
the present total pressure and the total pressure of a previous moment.
the present dynamic pressure and the static pressure of a previous moment.
the present static pressure and the static pressure of a previous moment.
q.e: It measures the rate of climb or descent by comparing the instantaneous static pressure to the static pressure from a fraction of a second ago, delayed by a calibrated leak.

q.t: What values are usually marked with a red line on instrument displays?
q.e: A red line on aviation instruments always indicates an absolute operational limit (e.g., maximum speed, maximum temperature) that must not be exceeded.

q.t: The term "static pressure" is defined as pressure...
o: resulting from orderly flow of air particles.
q.e: Static pressure is the absolute pressure of the undisturbed ambient air, uninfluenced by the motion of the aircraft.

q.t: The altimeter's reference scale is set to airfield pressure (QFE). What indication is shown during the flight?
q.e: When QFE is set, the altimeter displays the vertical distance (height) above the specific airfield's reference point.

q.t: A vertical speed indicator connected to a too big equalizing tank results in...
q.e: A larger equalizing tank (reservoir) would delay the pressure equalization longer than designed, causing the differential pressure to be greater and the indication to be exaggerated (too high).

q.t: A vertical speed indicator measures the difference between...
o: instantaneous total pressure and previous total pressure.
instantaneous static pressure and previous static pressure.
q.e: This is the fundamental principle of the VSI – comparing immediate static pressure to delayed (previous) static pressure.

q.t: The purpose of the drag lines of the parachute is ...
o: To transfer the carrying force of the balloon in the top opening area.
To transfer the force from the pull rope to the parachute.
To keep the parachute in the center of the top opening.
To transfer the force from the pull rope to the free-balloon hull.
q.e: Drag lines (or centering lines) ensure that the parachute valve remains centered over the top opening of the balloon envelope.

q.t: The towing rope of a gas balloon can be found on
q.e: The towing rope is traditionally located on the side of the rip panel to aid in deflation and control during landing.

q.t: The density of helium gas under standard conditions is:
q.e: The density of helium is approximately 0.1786 kg/m³ under standard conditions, which is typically rounded to 0.2 kg/m³ in standard basic aviation questions.

q.t: How will the sag of the pull rope change during descent?
q.e: During descent, aerodynamic forces on the balloon envelope push it upward relative to the basket, tightening the internal lines and decreasing the sag of the pull rope.

q.t: What is the purpose of the closing rope of a gas balloon?
q.e: The closing rope is used to tie off or close the appendix (the bottom opening) of the gas balloon during specific ground operations or inflation.

q.t: The emergency opening of a gas balloon is located where?
o: to the side of the appendix
to the side of the valve
q.e: The emergency opening (or rip panel slit) in a gas balloon is typically located near or to the side of the appendix for specific venting needs.

q.t: The minimum length of the towing rope is:
q.e: For standard gas balloon operations, the towing rope (trail rope) is required to have a minimum length, commonly 50 meters, to effectively slow the balloon via ground friction before landing.

q.t: A gas balloon has to be equipped with which tethers?
q.e: Standard operational regulations for gas balloons dictate specific tethering setups, typically 1 at 30 meters or 3 at 10 meters for ground handling.

q.t: The burst of a hydrogen pressure line may result in what risk?
o: The risk of hydrogen collecting in the basket and causing breath shortness.
The risk of hydrogen self-igniting and burning with a bright flame.
The risk of hydrogen dissipating to the atmosphere and poisening the air
The risk of hydrogen self-igniting and burning with invisible flame.
q.e: Hydrogen burns with a very pale, almost invisible flame in daylight. A burst pressurized line can cause self-ignition due to static electricity or friction.

q.t: The assembly of the panels to the hull of a web-less gas balloon is done ...
q.e: Modern web-less gas balloon envelopes are typically constructed from synthetic materials joined by high-frequency welding to ensure gas-tight seams.

q.t: What technical measure provides electric conductivity to the hull ropes of a web-less gas balloon?
q.e: To prevent the dangerous buildup of static electricity (especially with hydrogen), embedded steel threads or filaments are woven into the ropes to provide electrical grounding.

q.t: The rotational axis of the Earth runs through the...
o: geographic North Pole and on the geographic South Pole.
magnetic north pole and on the magnetic south pole.
geographic North Pole and on the magnetic south pole.
magnetic north pole and on the geographic South Pole.
q.e: The Earth rotates around its polar axis, which by definition passes exactly through the geographic North and South Poles.

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the polar axis of the Earth?
o: The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is at an angle of 23.5° to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is at an angle of 66.5° to the plane of the equator
q.e: The geographic polar axis is perfectly perpendicular (90 degrees) to the plane of the geographic equator.

q.t: Which approximate, geometrical form describes the shape of the Earth best for navigation systems?
q.e: For precise navigation (like GPS/WGS-84), the Earth is best modeled as an oblate spheroid or Ellipsoid, because it bulges slightly at the equator. (Note: Often translated poorly in charts as 'Sphere of ecliptical shape', but standard navigation theory uses Ellipsoid).

q.t: The shortest distance between two points on Earth is represented by a part of...
q.e: A great circle represents the intersection of the Earth's surface with a plane passing through the Earth's center, forming the shortest path between any two points.

q.t: The circumference of the Earth at the equator is approximately...
q.e: One degree of latitude equals 60 NM. Since the Earth is 360 degrees around, 360 * 60 = 21,600 NM.

q.t: What is the difference in latitude between A (12°53'30"N) and B (07°34'30"S)?
q.e: Since they are in different hemispheres, you add the latitudes: 12°53'30" + 07°34'30" = 19°87'60" = 20°28'00".

q.t: Where are the two polar circles?
o: north and south of the poles
23.5° north and south of the equator
23.5° north and south of the poles
q.e: The polar circles (Arctic and Antarctic) are located at approximately 66.5° N/S, which is 23.5° from the respective geographic poles.

q.t: What is the distance between the parallels of latitude 48°N and 49°N along a meridian line?
q.e: Along any meridian (longitude line), one degree of latitude equals exactly 60 Nautical Miles.

q.t: What distance corresponds to one degree difference in latitude along any degree of longitude?
q.e: By definition, one minute of latitude equals 1 Nautical Mile. Therefore, one degree (60 minutes) equals 60 NM.

q.t: Point A on the Earth's surface lies exactly on the parallel of latitude of 47°50'27"N. Which point is exactly 240 NM north of A?
q.e: 240 NM north equals 240 minutes of latitude, which is exactly 4 degrees. 47° + 4° = 51°50'27"N.

q.t: What is the distance between the two parallels of longitude 150°E and 151°E along the equator?
q.e: At the equator, the distance between degrees of longitude is at its maximum and equals 60 NM per degree, identical to degrees of latitude.

q.t: What is the great circle distance between two points A and B on the equator when the difference between the two associated meridians is exactly one degree of longitude?
q.e: The equator is a great circle itself, and 1 degree of longitude along the equator spans exactly 60 NM.

q.t: Assume two arbitrary points A and B on the same parallel of latitude, but not on the equator. Point A is located on 010°E and point B on 020°E. The rumb line distance between A and B is always...
q.e: The distance of 10 degrees longitude at the equator is 600 NM. Since parallels of latitude get smaller towards the poles, the distance for 10 degrees will always be less than 600 NM.

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 20° of longitude?
q.e: The Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour. Therefore, 20 degrees takes (20 / 15) = 1.33 hours, which is 1 hour and 20 minutes.

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 10° of longitude?
q.e: The Earth rotates 15 degrees in 60 minutes, which is 4 minutes per degree. 10 degrees * 4 minutes = 40 minutes (0:40 h).

q.t: With Central European Summer Time (CEST) given as UTC+2, what UTC time corresponds to 1600 CEST?
q.e: To find UTC, subtract the offset from local time: 1600 CEST - 2 hours = 1400 UTC.

q.t: UTC is...
o: a local time in Central Europe.
local mean time at a specific point on Earth.
an obligatory time used in aviation.
q.e: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the universal standard time used across all global aviation to prevent timezone confusion.

q.t: With Central European Time (CET) given as UTC+1, what UTC time corresponds to 1700 CET?
q.e: 1700 CET minus the 1 hour offset equals 1600 UTC.

q.t: Vienna (LOWW) is located at 016° 34'E, Salzburg (LOWS) at 013° 00'E. The latitude of both positions can be considered as equal. What is the difference of sunrise and sunset times, expressed in UTC, between Wien and Salzburg?
o: In Vienna the sunrise and sunset are about 4 minutes later than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise and sunset are about 14 minutes earlier than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise is 4 minutes later and sunset is 4 minutes earlier than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise is 14 minutes earlier and sunset is 14 minutes later than in Salzburg
q.e: Vienna is further East by about 3.5 degrees. 3.5 degrees * 4 minutes/degree = 14 minutes. Since it is further East, the sun rises and sets earlier there.

q.t: The term 'civil twilight' is defined as...
o: the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 12 degrees or less below the true horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 6 degrees or less below the apparent horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 6 degrees or less below the true horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 12 degrees or less below the apparent horizon.
q.e: Civil twilight begins/ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the true (ideal) horizon.

q.t: Given: TC: 179°; WCA: -12°; VAR: 004° E; DEV: +002°. What are MH and MC?
The term 'magnetic course' (MC) is defined as...
o: the angle between true north and the course line.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the magnetic north pole.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographic North Pole.
the angle between magnetic north and the course line.
q.e: Magnetic Course is the intended path of the aircraft relative to Magnetic North.

q.t: The term 'True Course' (TC) is defined as...
o: the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographic North Pole.
the angle between true north and the course line.
tthe angle between magnetic north and the course line.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the magnetic north pole.
q.e: True Course is the intended path of the aircraft measured relative to True (Geographic) North.

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are TH and VAR?
q.e: TH = TC + WCA = 183 + 11 = 194°. VAR = TH - MH = 194 - 198 = -4° (which means 4° West).

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are the TH and the DEV?
Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are the VAR and the DEV?
Where does the inclination reach its lowest value?
q.e: Magnetic inclination (dip) is 0 degrees (lowest value) at the magnetic equator, where the magnetic field lines are perfectly parallel to the Earth's surface.

q.t: The angle between compass north and magnetic north is called...
q.e: Deviation is the error induced in the compass by the aircraft's own local magnetic fields, creating an angle between Magnetic North and Compass North.

q.t: Which direction corresponds to 'compass north' (CN)?
o: The most northerly part of the magnetic compass in the aircraft, where the reading takes place
The direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographical North Pole
The angle between the aircraft heading and magnetic north
The direction to which the direct reading compass aligns due to earth's and aircraft's magnetic fields
q.e: Compass North is the actual direction the needle points, which is a combination of the Earth's magnetic field and local aircraft interference (deviation).

q.t: The term 'isogonal' or 'isogonic line' is defined as a line on an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the same value of...
q.e: Isogonic lines connect points of equal magnetic variation (declination), which helps pilots convert between true and magnetic headings.

q.t: The term 'agonic line' is defined as a line on Earth or an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the...
q.e: An agonic line is a specific isogonic line where the magnetic variation is exactly zero (True North and Magnetic North align perfectly).

q.t: Which are the official basic units for horizontal distances used in aeronautical navigation and their abbreviations?
q.e: Standard ICAO aviation charts use Nautical Miles (NM) for distance, and occasionally kilometers (km) depending on the region or specific VFR chart standard.

q.t: 1000 ft equal...
q.e: One foot is approximately 0.3048 meters. Therefore, 1000 feet is roughly equal to 300 meters.

q.t: 5500 m equal...
q.e: 5500 meters divided by 0.3048 m/ft equals approximately 18,044 feet, heavily rounded to 18,000 feet (FL180, a common pressure transition marker).

q.t: Electronic devices on board of an aeroplane have influence on the...
q.e: Electronic devices emit electromagnetic fields, which interfere directly with the magnetic needle of the direct reading compass, causing deviation.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Mercator chart?
o: The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
q.e: In a Mercator projection, rhumb lines are straight (constant heading), but great circles curve. The scale distorts (increases) significantly as you move toward the poles.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Lambert conformal chart?
o: The chart is conformal and nearly true to scale
Great circles are depicted as straight lines and the chart is an equal-area projection
Rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines and the chart is conformal
The chart is conformal and an equal-area projection
q.e: Lambert Conformal Conic charts are widely used for aviation because a straight line closely approximates a great circle, angles are preserved (conformal), and scale is nearly constant across the map.

q.t: The distance between two airports is 220 NM. On an aeronautical navigation chart the pilot measures 40.7 cm for this distance. The chart scale is...
A distance of 7.5 cm on an aeronautical chart represents a distance of 60.745 NM in reality. What is the chart scale?
An aircraft travels 100 km in 56 minutes. The ground speed (GS) equals...
q.e: Speed = Distance / Time. 100 km / (56 / 60) hours = 107.14 km/h.

q.t: How many satellites are necessary for a precise and verified three-dimensional determination of the position?
q.e: A GPS receiver requires at least 4 satellites to resolve the 4 variables: latitude, longitude, altitude (3D), and time receiver clock error.

q.t: When using a GPS for tracking to the next waypoint, a deviation indication is shown by a vertical bar and dots to the left and to the right of the bar. What statement describes the correct interpretation of the display?
o: The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection is +-10 NM.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection is +-10°
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
q.e: GPS CDI (Course Deviation Indicator) bars show linear cross-track distance (e.g., in NM), not angular degrees like a VOR. The sensitivity (full scale) changes depending on whether in Enroute, Terminal, or Approach mode.

q.t: What is meant by the term "terrestrial navigation"?
o: Orientation by instrument readings during visual flight
Orientation by ground features during visual flight
Orientation by GPS during visual flight
Orientation by ground celestial object during visual flight
q.e: Terrestrial (or pilotage) navigation involves plotting a route using visible landmarks and physical ground features on the Earth's surface.

q.t: What ground features should preferrably be used for orientation during visual flight?
q.e: Large, continuous features like major rivers, highways, and railroads are easiest to spot from altitude and form excellent "catching lines" or tracking references.

q.t: In which situations should a pilot use blind transmissions?
o: When a transmission containing important navigational or technical information is to be sent to several stations at the same time
When a pilot has flown into cloud or fog unintentionally and would like to request navigational assistance
When no radio communication can be established with the appropriate aeronautical station, but evidence exists that transmissions are received at that ground unit
When the traffic situation at an airport allows transmission of information which does not need to be acknowledged
q.e: Blind transmissions are used when a pilot cannot receive responses from a ground station but has reason to believe the transmissions are being received (e.g., during radio failure). The pilot transmits on the appropriate frequency, beginning with 'Transmitting blind' so the ground station knows no reply is expected.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term 'abeam'?
q.e: ABM is the ICAO abbreviation for 'abeam' — meaning a position at 90° to the aircraft's heading, either to port (left) or starboard (right). This is a standard positional reference used in ATC communications and flight plans.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term 'visual flight rules'?
q.e: VFR stands for Visual Flight Rules. VMC stands for Visual Meteorological Conditions (the weather conditions under which VFR may be conducted). These are distinct: VFR is the set of rules, VMC is the weather standard that must be met to follow those rules.

q.t: Which abbreviation is used for the term 'obstacle'?
q.e: OBST is the ICAO standard abbreviation for 'obstacle'. It is used in NOTAMs, charts, and ATC communications to indicate man-made or natural objects that may constitute a hazard to aircraft navigation (towers, cranes, tall buildings, etc.).

q.t: What does the abbreviation 'FIS' stand for?
q.e: FIS stands for Flight Information Service. It is a service provided to give advice and information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flights, including weather, NOTAMs, and traffic information. It does not provide ATC clearances.

q.t: What does the abbreviation 'FIR' stand for?
q.e: FIR stands for Flight Information Region. It is an airspace of defined dimensions within which Flight Information Service and Alerting Service are provided. FIRs are the fundamental units of international airspace structure established by ICAO.

q.t: What does the abbreviation 'H24' stand for?
q.e: H24 indicates continuous operation — 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It is used in AIP and NOTAM publications to indicate that a service (e.g., AFIS, ATC, fuel) is available around the clock without interruption.

q.t: What does the abbreviation 'HX' stand for?
q.e: HX indicates no specific operational hours — the facility or service has no fixed schedule. Other standard time designators include H24 (continuous), HJ (sunrise to sunset), and HN (sunset to sunrise). HX means the hours are irregular or on-demand.

q.t: The altimeter has to be set to what value in order to show zero on ground?
q.e: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at the aerodrome reference point. When set on the altimeter sub-scale, the altimeter reads zero (height = 0) when the aircraft is on the ground at that aerodrome. QNH causes the altimeter to read the aerodrome elevation when on the ground.

q.t: Which altitude is displayed on the altimeter when set to a specific QNH?
o: Altitude in relation to the 1013.25 hPa datum
Altitude in relation to the highest elevation within 10 km
Altitude in relation to mean sea level
Altitude in relation to the air pressure at the reference airfield
q.e: QNH is the local sea-level pressure derived from the station pressure. When the altimeter is set to QNH, it reads the aircraft's altitude above mean sea level (AMSL). This allows comparison with aerodrome and terrain elevations published in MSL.

q.t: Which altitude is displayed on the altimeter when set to a specific QFE?
o: Altitude in relation to mean sea level
Altitude in relation to the highest elevation within 10 km
Altitude in relation to the 1013.25 hPa datum
Altitude in relation to the air pressure at the reference airfield
q.e: QFE is the pressure at the aerodrome reference point. Setting QFE on the altimeter causes it to read zero on the ground, and heights above the aerodrome during flight (height AGL relative to that aerodrome). It is used at some military aerodromes and for circuit flying.

q.t: What is the correct term for a message used for air traffic control?
q.e: ATC messages are classified as 'flight safety messages' — they have the highest communications priority because they relate directly to the safety of aircraft in flight. The priority order is: distress, urgency, direction finding, flight safety, meteorological, then flight regularity messages.

q.t: Distress messages are messages...
o: sent by a pilot or an aircraft operating agency which have an imminent meaning for aircraft in flight.
concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
concerning the operation or maintenance of facilities which are important for the safety and regularity of flight operations.
q.e: Distress messages (MAYDAY) concern aircraft or persons facing a grave and imminent threat requiring immediate assistance. They have the highest priority in radio communications. The distress signal MAYDAY is repeated three times before the message content.

q.t: Urgency messages are messages...
o: concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
concerning the operation or maintenance of facilities essential for the safety or regularity of aircraft operation.
sent by a pilot or an aircraft operating agency which have an imminent meaning for aircraft in flight.
q.e: Urgency messages (PAN PAN) concern the safety of an aircraft, vessel, or person in sight requiring assistance, but not involving an immediate threat to life. The urgency signal PAN PAN is repeated three times before the message. It has lower priority than distress but higher than all other messages.

q.t: Regularity messages are messages...
o: concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
sent by an aircraft operating agency or an aircraft of immediate concern to an aircraft in flight.
concerning the operation or maintenance of facilities essential for the safety or regularity of aircraft operation.
q.e: Regularity messages concern the operation or maintenance of facilities essential for the safety or regularity of aircraft operations — for example, messages about navigation aids being unserviceable. They have lower priority than distress, urgency, direction finding, flight safety, and meteorological messages.

q.t: Which of the following messages has the highest priority?
q.e: ATC instructions such as 'Turn left' are flight safety messages, which have higher priority than informational messages like QNH, wind, or navigation assistance requests. Flight safety messages (ATC clearances and instructions) rank above meteorological and flight regularity messages.

q.t: What is the correct way to transmit the call sign HB-YKM?
q.e: Using the ICAO phonetic alphabet: H = Hotel, B = Bravo, Y = Yankee, K = Kilo, M = Mike. 'Yuliett' is the incorrect spelling (should be Juliet for J, not Y which is Yankee). 'Mikro' is not a standard phonetic word. The correct transmission is Hotel Bravo Yankee Kilo Mike.

q.t: What is the correct way to transmit the call sign OE-JVK?
q.e: Using the ICAO phonetic alphabet: O = Oscar, E = Echo, J = Juliett, V = Victor, K = Kilo. 'Omega' is not a standard phonetic letter (O is Oscar). 'Jankee' is not correct (J is Juliett). 'Kilogramm' is not the standard word (K is Kilo). Correct: Oscar Echo Juliett Victor Kilo.

q.t: An altitude of 4500 ft is transmitted as...
q.e: ICAO phraseology for altitudes: 4500 ft is transmitted as 'four thousand five hundred'. Altitudes are spoken as thousands and hundreds: e.g., 4500 = 'four thousand five hundred', not as individual digits. FL450 would be 'flight level four five zero'.

q.t: A heading of 285 degrees is correctly transmitted as...
q.e: Headings and tracks are transmitted as individual digits in ICAO phraseology: 285 is 'two eight five'. This prevents confusion with numbers that could be misheard — 'two hundred eighty-five' could be ambiguous. Runway numbers follow the same convention.

q.t: A frequency of 119.500 MHz is correctly transmitted as...
o: one one niner decimal five zero.
one one niner tousand decimal five zero.
one one niner decimal five zero zero.
q.e: Frequencies are transmitted with all significant digits: 119.500 MHz = 'one one niner decimal five zero zero' would be for 8.33 kHz spacing aircraft. For standard 25 kHz spacing, 119.500 is 'one one niner decimal five zero'. The trailing zero after the decimal is included per ICAO Doc 9432.

q.t: The directional information '12 o'clock' is correctly transmitted as...
q.e: Clock position references (used for traffic advisories) are transmitted as 'one two o'clock', not 'twelve o'clock'. ICAO phraseology uses the individual digit format with 'o'clock' appended: 12 o'clock = 'one two o'clock', 3 o'clock = 'three o'clock'.

q.t: Times are transmitted as...
q.e: All aviation time is expressed in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), formerly known as GMT. This universal time standard eliminates confusion caused by different time zones and daylight saving time variations across international flights. ICAO Annex 2 mandates the use of UTC in aviation.

q.t: If there is any doubt about ambiguity, a time of 1620 is to be transmitted as...
o: one tousand six hundred two zero.
q.e: To avoid ambiguity, times are transmitted as four digits in ICAO phraseology: 1620 UTC = 'one six two zero'. If only the minutes are sufficiently clear from context, just the last two digits may be used. Full four-digit format is always acceptable and recommended when in doubt.

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase 'Roger'?
o: Permission for proposed action is granted
I understand your message and will comply with it
An error has been made in this transmission. The correct version is...
I have received all of your last transmission
q.e: Roger' means 'I have received all of your last transmission.' It only confirms receipt, not understanding or compliance. It should not be confused with 'Wilco' (I understand and will comply) or 'Affirm' (yes). Using 'Roger' as confirmation of an ATC clearance is not correct — 'Wilco' or a full readback should be used.

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase 'Correction'?
o: Permission for proposed action is granted
An error has been made in this transmission. The correct version is...
I have received all of your last transmission
I understand your message and will comply with it
q.e: Correction' is used when an error has been made in a previous transmission. The correct information follows: 'Correction, [correct version].' This is important for accuracy in ATC communications where incorrect information could have safety implications.

q.t: What is the meaning of the phrase 'Approved'?
o: An error has been made in this transmission. The correct version is...
Permission for proposed action is granted
I have received all of your last transmission
I understand your message and will comply with it
q.e: Approved' means 'Permission for the proposed action is granted.' It is the standard ICAO phrase used by controllers to give permission. It is distinct from 'Affirm' (yes), 'Roger' (received), and 'Wilco' (will comply).

q.t: Which phrase does a pilot use when he/she wants to check the readability of his/her transmission?
q.e: How do you read?' is the standard ICAO phrase used to request a readability check. The response uses the readability scale from 1 (unreadable) to 5 (perfectly readable): 'I read you [number].' This is used when signal quality is uncertain.

q.t: Which phrase is used by a pilot when he wants to fly through controlled airspace?
q.e: Request' is the standard ICAO phraseology word used when a pilot is asking ATC for something, such as permission to enter controlled airspace, a frequency change, or a service. It replaces informal words like 'want', 'would like', or non-standard alternatives.

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot if a transmission is to be answered with 'yes'?
q.e: Affirm' is the correct ICAO standard word for 'yes'. 'Affirmative' is used in some non-ICAO systems (e.g., military). 'Roger' means 'received', not 'yes'. Simply saying 'yes' is not standard phraseology. 'Affirm' is short, unambiguous, and universally understood in aviation communications.

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot if a transmission is to be answered with 'no'?
q.e: Negative' is the ICAO standard word for 'no.' It is clear and unambiguous on radio. Simply saying 'no' is not standard phraseology. 'Negative' is also used to correct information: 'Negative, our fuel state is...'

q.t: Which phrase is to be used when a pilot wants the tower to know that he is ready for take-off?
q.e: Ready for departure' is the correct phrase when a pilot has completed all pre-take-off checks and is ready to take off. 'Request take-off' is not standard phraseology — ATC issues take-off clearances, and pilots indicate readiness with 'Ready for departure'.

q.t: What phrase is used by a pilot to inform the tower about a go-around?
q.e: Going around' is the standard ICAO phrase used by a pilot to inform ATC that they are discontinuing an approach and executing a go-around (missed approach). This immediately alerts ATC so they can sequence other traffic and issue appropriate instructions.

q.t: What is the call sign of the aerodrome control?
q.e: The aerodrome control service (which controls aircraft in the air in the aerodrome traffic zone and on the runway) uses the call sign suffix 'Tower' (e.g., 'Frankfurt Tower'). 'Ground' is used for surface movement control; 'Approach' for approach control; 'Radar' for radar services.

q.t: What is the call sign of the surface movement control?
q.e: Surface movement control (responsible for aircraft and vehicles taxiing on the aerodrome manoeuvring area) uses the call sign suffix 'Ground' (e.g., 'Heathrow Ground'). The Tower controls aircraft on and in the vicinity of the runway, while Ground controls all ground movements except on active runways.

q.t: What is the call sign of the flight information service?
q.e: FIS units use the call sign suffix 'Information' (e.g., 'Langen Information', 'Scottish Information'). This distinguishes them from ATC units which use Tower, Approach, Radar, or Control. FIS provides information but does not issue ATC clearances.

q.t: What is the correct abbreviation of the call sign D-EAZF?
q.e: The abbreviated call sign uses the prefix (nationality letter) and the last two characters of the full registration: D-EAZF abbreviates to D-ZF or just 'DZF' on radio. The first letter(s) after the hyphen may be omitted once two-way communication is established on the abbreviated form.

q.t: In what case is the pilot allowed to abbreviate the call sign of his aircraft?
o: After the ground station has used the abbreviation
If there is little traffic in the traffic circuit
After passing the first reporting point
q.e: A pilot may only use an abbreviated call sign after the ground station has first used the abbreviated form. Once the ground station abbreviates the call sign (e.g., 'DZF, cleared to land'), the pilot may continue using the abbreviation. Using abbreviations without this initiation risks confusion with similarly abbreviated call signs.

q.t: What is the correct way of using the aircraft call sign at first contact?
o: Using the last two characters only
Using the first two characters only
Using the first three characters only
q.e: On first contact with any ATC unit, pilots must use the full aircraft call sign. This ensures unambiguous identification, especially when multiple aircraft with similar abbreviated call signs may be operating. Abbreviation is only permitted after the ground station initiates it.

q.t: What is the correct way of establishing radio communication between D-EAZF and Dusseldorf Tower?
q.e: The correct ICAO format for initial radio contact is: [called station] [calling station], i.e., 'Dusseldorf Tower, D-EAZF.' The called station comes first, then the calling station's full call sign. 'Over' is added if a response is expected but is sometimes omitted in practice.

q.t: What does a readability of 1 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable now and then
The transmission is readable but with difficulty
q.e: The ICAO readability scale runs from 1 to 5: 1 = Unreadable, 2 = Readable now and then, 3 = Readable but with difficulty, 4 = Readable, 5 = Perfectly readable. A readability of 1 means the transmission cannot be understood.

q.t: What does a readability of 2 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable but with difficulty
The transmission is readable now and then
q.e: Readability 2 = 'Readable now and then' on the ICAO 1-5 readability scale. This means the transmission is intermittently intelligible but not reliable enough for safe communication. The pilot or controller would request the other party to repeat or relay.

q.t: What does a readability of 3 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable now and then
The transmission is readable but with difficulty
q.e: Readability 3 = 'Readable but with difficulty' on the ICAO readability scale. The transmission can be understood with effort but errors are possible. Important clearances should be repeated and verified when readability is 3 or below.

q.t: What does a readability of 5 indicate?
o: The transmission is readable but with difficulty
The transmission is readable now and then
q.e: Readability 5 = 'Perfectly readable' — the best possible signal quality on the ICAO 1-5 scale. Clear, unambiguous, with no distortion or interference. This is the expected standard for normal VHF communications within range.

q.t: Which information from a ground station does not require readback?
q.e: Wind information does not require a formal readback — it is advisory information for the pilot. However, items that MUST be read back include: ATC route clearances, runway in use, altimeter settings, SSR codes, clearances to enter/cross/backtrack on active runways, altitude restrictions, and headings/speeds.

q.t: Which information from a ground station does not require readback?
q.e: Traffic information (e.g., 'traffic 2 o'clock, 3 miles') is advisory and does not require a formal readback — a simple 'Roger' or 'Looking' suffices. Taxi instructions, headings, and altimeter settings all require proper readbacks per ICAO and EASA requirements.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging the instruction 'DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead until 2500 feet before turning right heading 220 degrees, wind 090 degrees, 5 knots, runway 12, cleared for take-off'?
o: DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, then turn right heading 220, runway 12, cleared for take-off
DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, then turn right heading 220, 090 degrees, 5 knots, cleared for take-off
DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, wilco, heading 220 degrees, 090 degrees, 5 knots, cleared for take-off
DZF after lift-off climb straight ahead 2500 feet, then turn right heading 220, 090 degrees, 5 knots
q.e: The readback must include: the instruction elements (altitude, turn, heading), the runway, and the clearance. Wind information does not require readback. The runway number and 'cleared for take-off' must be read back as they are critical safety items. Option A correctly reads back all mandatory elements without the wind.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging the instruction 'Next report PAH'?
q.e: Wilco' (from 'will comply') is correct when acknowledging a reporting instruction. It means 'I have received and understood your message and will comply with it.' 'Roger' only means received. 'Report PAH' is a partial readback but 'Wilco' is acceptable for simple instructions. Option D (Report PAH) is also a valid readback.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging the instruction 'Squawk 4321, Call Bremen Radar on 131.325'?
q.e: Both the squawk code and the frequency must be read back as they are safety-critical items. The correct readback is 'Squawk 4321, 131.325' (the frequency). Just saying 'Roger' or 'Wilco' is insufficient for items requiring mandatory readback. The squawk code is mandatory readback per EASA.

q.t: What is the correct way of acknowledging 'You are now entering airspace Delta'?
q.e: Roger' is appropriate here as this is an advisory/informational message from ATC, not an instruction requiring compliance. The phrase confirms that the message was received. 'Wilco' would imply a compliance action is required, which is not the case for an informational message.

q.t: What does a cloud coverage of 'FEW' mean in a METAR weather report?
q.e: Cloud coverage in METAR is reported in oktas (eighths of sky covered): FEW = 1-2 oktas, SCT (Scattered) = 3-4 oktas, BKN (Broken) = 5-7 oktas, OVC (Overcast) = 8 oktas. SKC or NCD means no cloud detected/reported.

q.t: What does a cloud coverage of 'SCT' mean in a METAR weather report?
q.e: SCT = Scattered, covering 3-4 oktas (3-4 eighths) of the sky. The METAR cloud coverage codes are: SKC/NCD = nil, FEW = 1-2, SCT = 3-4, BKN = 5-7, OVC = 8. SCT does not constitute a 'ceiling' as it covers less than half the sky.

q.t: What does a cloud coverage of 'BKN' mean in a METAR weather report?
q.e: BKN = Broken, covering 5-7 oktas of the sky. BKN constitutes a 'ceiling' as it covers more than half the sky (more than 4 oktas). The lowest BKN or OVC layer determines the reported ceiling. BKN allows some sky to be seen between cloud masses.

q.t: In what case is visibility transmitted in meters?
q.e: In METAR and ATIS, visibility up to and including 9999 m (approximately 10 km) is transmitted in metres (e.g., '4000' = 4000 m visibility). When visibility is 10 km or greater, it is reported as '9999' or as a distance in km (depending on regional conventions).

q.t: In what cases is visibility transmitted in kilometers?
q.e: In R/T phraseology (not METAR coding), visibility greater than 10 km is reported in kilometres. Below 10 km, visibility is reported in metres to give more precision (e.g., '4000 metres', '800 metres'). In METAR coding, '9999' represents 10 km or more visibility.

q.t: What information is broadcasted on a VOLMET frequency?
q.e: VOLMET (from French 'vol météo') is a continuous broadcast of meteorological information for aircraft in flight, transmitted on specific VHF/HF frequencies. It provides METAR/SPECI reports and TAFs for major airports to help pilots plan and update weather assessments en route.

q.t: How can you obtain meteorological information concerning airports during a cross-country flight?
q.e: VOLMET is the primary source of current aerodrome meteorological information available to pilots in flight via VHF radio. METAR is the format/content of the report but requires ground access. AIRMET is for significant en-route weather below FL100. GAMET is a forecast for low-level flights.

q.t: Which transponder code indicates a radio failure?
q.e: 7600 = radio failure (loss of communication). The three emergency/special codes are: 7700 = emergency, 7600 = radio failure, 7500 = unlawful interference (hijacking). 7000 is the standard VFR conspicuity code used in uncontrolled airspace in Europe when no other code is assigned.

q.t: What is the correct phrase to begin a blind transmission?
q.e: The correct ICAO phrase to begin a blind transmission is 'Transmitting blind' followed by the recipient's call sign. This alerts the ground station (which may be receiving even if the pilot cannot receive replies) that no response is expected and that the pilot is aware of the one-way communication.

q.t: On what frequency shall a blind transmission be made?
o: On a radar frequency of the lower airspace
q.e: Blind transmissions should be made on the current (last used or appropriate assigned) frequency, where the ground station may still be receiving even if the pilot cannot receive responses. After several attempts, other relevant frequencies (including the emergency frequency 121.5 MHz) may be tried.

q.t: How often shall a blind transmission be made?
q.e: ICAO phraseology specifies that blind transmissions should be made three times on the appropriate frequency. The complete transmission sequence is: 'Transmitting blind [3 times], [message content] [3 times].' Each attempt gives the ground station multiple opportunities to receive.

q.t: In what situation is it appropriate to set the transponder code 7600?
q.e: 7600 is the transponder code for radio communication failure (loss of radio). It alerts ATC that the aircraft has lost radio but the crew is still operating the aircraft normally. 7500 is for hijacking, 7700 for emergency, and 7000 for normal VFR.

q.t: What is the correct course of action when experiencing a radio failure in class D airspace?
o: The flight has to be continued above 5000 feet complying with VFR flight rules or the airspace has to be left by the shortest route
The flight has to be continued according to the last clearance complying with VFR flight rules or the airspace has to be left using a standard routing
The flight has to be continued according to the last clearance complying with VFR rules or the airspace has to be left by the shortest route
The flight has to be continued above 5000 feet complying with VFR flight rules or the airspace has to be left using a standard routing
q.e: In case of radio failure in Class D airspace, the pilot should continue according to the last ATC clearance while complying with VFR rules, or leave the airspace by the shortest possible route. This minimises conflict with other traffic while maintaining a predictable flight path for ATC.

q.t: Under what conditions may class D airspace be entered with a radio failure?
o: It is the aerodrome of departure
There are other aircraft in the aerodrome circuit
q.e: Class D airspace may be entered with radio failure if it is the destination aerodrome — the pilot needs to land there. In this case, the pilot should follow the light signals procedure. For transit of Class D airspace with radio failure, the pilot should avoid entry unless the destination is within that airspace.

q.t: Which phrase is to be repeated three times before transmitting an urgency message?
q.e: The urgency signal 'PAN PAN' is spoken three times before an urgency message: 'Pan Pan, Pan Pan, Pan Pan, [message].' This follows ICAO Annex 10 and Doc 9432. MAYDAY (spoken three times) precedes distress messages. Neither 'Help' nor 'Urgent' are standard ICAO signals.

q.t: Urgency messages are defined as...
o: messages concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
messages concerning urgent spare parts which are needed for a continuation of flight and which need to be ordered in advance.
messages concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
information concerning the apron personnel and which imply an imminent danger to landing aircraft.
q.e: Urgency messages concern the safety of an aircraft, watercraft, or other vehicle or person observed in distress but not requiring immediate life-saving assistance. This contrasts with distress messages (MAYDAY) which involve grave and imminent threat to life.

q.t: Distress messages contain...
o: information concerning the safety of an aircraft, a watercraft or some other vehicle or person in sight.
information concerning aircraft and their passengers which face a grave and imminent threat and require immediate assistance.
information concerning urgent spare parts which are required for a continuation of flight and which have to be ordered in advance.
information concerning the apron personnel and which imply an imminent danger to landing aircraft.
q.e: Distress messages (MAYDAY) concern situations where aircraft and/or persons are threatened by grave and imminent danger and require immediate assistance. This is the highest priority communication in aviation. The key words are 'grave', 'imminent', and 'immediate assistance'.

q.t: What is the correct frequency for an initial distress message?
q.e: Initial distress calls should be made on the current operating frequency — the frequency currently in use when the emergency occurs. This ensures immediate reception by ATC or other aircraft in the area. If no response, the pilot should try the emergency frequency 121.5 MHz.

q.t: What kind of information should be included in an urgency message?
o: Nature of problem or observation, important information for support, departure aerodrome, information about position, heading and altitude
Intended routing, important information for support, intentions of the pilot, departure aerodrome, destination aerodrome, heading and altitude
Intended routing, important information for support, intentions of the pilot, information about position, departure aerodrome, heading and altitude
Nature of problem or observation, important information for support, intentions of the pilot, information about position, heading and altitude
q.e: An urgency (PAN PAN) message should include: nature of the problem/observation, important information to assist rescue services, pilot's intentions, aircraft position, heading, altitude, and any other relevant information. This gives rescuers what they need to respond effectively.

q.t: The correct transponder code for emergencies is...
q.e: 7700 is the transponder code for emergency. The three special codes are: 7700 = Emergency (MAYDAY/PAN PAN), 7600 = Radio communication failure, 7500 = Unlawful interference (hijacking). 7000 is the standard VFR conspicuity code in European airspace.

q.t: What is the correct designation of the frequency band from 118.000 to 136.975 MHz used for voice communication?
q.e: VHF (Very High Frequency) covers 30-300 MHz. Aviation voice communication uses 118-136.975 MHz, which is within the VHF band. VHF provides line-of-sight communication, so range depends on altitude. MF (Medium Frequency) is 300 kHz - 3 MHz; HF (High Frequency) is 3-30 MHz for long-range.

q.t: Which of the following factors affects the reception of VHF transmissions?
q.e: VHF signals travel in line-of-sight. Altitude is the main factor affecting VHF range — higher altitude means longer range as the radio horizon extends further. Twilight error and shoreline effect affect NDB/ADF signals, not VHF. The ionosphere reflects HF, not VHF.

q.t: What is the approximate speed of electromagnetic wave propagation?
q.e: Electromagnetic waves (including radio waves and light) travel at approximately 300,000 km/s (3 × 10⁸ m/s) in a vacuum. This is the universal constant 'c', the speed of light. In practical aviation communications, signals are considered instantaneous over normal ranges.

q.t: An ATIS is valid for...
q.e: ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) broadcasts are updated at regular intervals, typically every hour (60 minutes) or whenever there is a significant change in conditions. Each broadcast is identified by a sequential letter (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...). Pilots must obtain the current ATIS before requesting startup or clearance.

q.t: At time of take-off, ground wind speed is 3 m/s. Along take-off flight path, at a distance of 360 m obstacles erect up to 40 m. What is the minimum rate of climb to keep a clearance of 50 m above obstacles? (Consider double the ground wind speed for the flight path)
q.e: Wind speed for calculation = 2 × 3 = 6 m/s. Time to reach obstacles: 360m ÷ 6m/s = 60 s. Required height at obstacles: 40m + 50m = 90m. Rate of climb needed: 90m ÷ 60s = 1.5 m/s. But the balloon starts climbing immediately, so required ROC = 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5... Re-check: answer is 1.5 m/s per calculation, but question bank answer is 1 m/s. Using standard method: ROC = (obstacle height + clearance) / (distance / airspeed) = 90/60 = 1.5. The book answer is A (1 m/s) — verify with your instructor.

q.t: At time of take-off, ground wind speed is 3 m/s. Along take-off flight path, at a distance of 270 m obstacles erect up to 40 m. What is the minimum rate of climb to keep a clearance of 50 m above the obstacles? (Consider double the ground wind speed for the flight path)
q.e: Wind speed for calculation = 2 × 3 = 6 m/s. Time to reach obstacles = 270 ÷ 6 = 45 s. Required height = 40 + 50 = 90 m. Minimum ROC = 90 ÷ 45 = 2 m/s. Note: The book answer is C (1.5 m/s). Always verify calculation method with your training manual.

q.t: A cross-country flight is made using the ICAO 1:500,000 aeronautical chart. An overflight crosscheck shows that a distance of 6 cm in the chart has been passed within 9 minutes. After how many more minutes can the overflight of another waypoint at a chart distance of additional 4 cm be expected?
q.e: Speed = 6 cm in 9 min = 0.667 cm/min. Time for additional 4 cm = 4 ÷ 0.667 = 6 minutes. On a 1:500,000 chart, 1 cm = 5 km, so 4 cm = 20 km. Ground speed = 30 km/9 min = 200 km/h. Time for 20 km = 20/200 × 60 = 6 min.

q.t: At time of take-off, ground wind speed is 2 m/s. Along take-off flight path, at a distance of 320 m obstacles erect up to 30 m. What is the minimum rate of climb to keep a clearance of 50 m above the obstacles? (Consider double the ground wind speed for the flight path)
q.e: Wind speed for calculation = 2 × 2 = 4 m/s. Time to reach obstacles = 320 ÷ 4 = 80 s. Required height = 30 + 50 = 80 m. Minimum ROC = 80 ÷ 80 = 1 m/s.

q.t: A cross-country flight is made using the ICAO 1:500,000 aeronautical chart. A distance of 4 cm in the chart has been passed within 12 minutes. After how many more minutes can the overflight of another waypoint at a chart distance of additional 6 cm be expected?
q.e: Speed = 4 cm in 12 min = 0.333 cm/min. Time for additional 6 cm = 6 ÷ 0.333 = 18 minutes. On 1:500,000 chart: 4 cm = 20 km in 12 min = ground speed 100 km/h. Time for 6 cm (30 km) = 30/100 × 60 = 18 min.

q.t: While overflying a waypoint, it is stated that a distance of 2 NM has been taken 10 min. What will be the expected time of endurance for the complete distance of 18 NM?
q.e: Ground speed = 2 NM in 10 min = 12 NM/hour. Time for 18 NM = 18 ÷ (2/10) = 18 × 10/2 = 90 minutes. This is a simple proportional calculation: if 2 NM takes 10 min, 18 NM takes 90 min.

q.t: While overflying a waypoint, it is stated that a distance of 3 NM has been taken 10 min. What will be the expected time of endurance for the complete distance of 18 NM?
q.e: Ground speed = 3 NM in 10 min = 18 NM/hour. Time for 18 NM = 18 ÷ (3/10) = 18 × 10/3 = 60 minutes. Simple proportion: 3 NM/10 min → 18 NM/60 min.

q.t: After take-off with a balloon, obstacles at a distance of 300 m erect in expected flight path up to 40 m height. Rate of climb is expected with 1.5 m/s. What maximum actual wind speed can be accepted to maintain a clearance of 50 m above obstacles, assuming double the actual wind speed for calculation?
q.e: Required height at obstacles = 40 + 50 = 90 m. Time to climb 90 m at 1.5 m/s = 90 ÷ 1.5 = 60 s. Wind speed (double actual) = distance ÷ time = 300 ÷ 60 = 5 m/s. Actual wind = 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 m/s.

q.t: After take-off with a balloon, obstacles at a distance of 600 m erect in expected flight path up to 40 m height. Rate of climb is expected with 1.5 m/s. What maximum actual wind speed can be accepted to maintain a clearance of 50 m above obstacles, assuming double the actual wind speed for calculation?
q.e: Required height = 40 + 50 = 90 m. Time to climb 90 m at 1.5 m/s = 60 s. Wind speed (doubled) = 600 ÷ 60 = 10 m/s. Actual wind = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m/s.

q.t: While overflying a waypoint, it is stated that a distance of 3 NM has been taken 10 min. What will be the expected time of endurance for the remaining distance of 18 NM?
q.e: Ground speed = 3 NM / 10 min. Time for 18 NM = 18 × 10 / 3 = 60 minutes. Same calculation as question 7 — consistent answer of 60 min for 18 NM at 3 NM/10min speed.

q.t: The maximum number of passengers can be found...
q.e: The operating handbook (Flight Manual / Pilot's Operating Handbook) contains all operational limitations including maximum passenger numbers, weight limitations, and performance data. The certificate of registration identifies the aircraft; the airworthiness certificate confirms its condition; the logbook records flight history.

q.t: The Empty Mass of a gas balloon includes:
o: Ballast packages, basket, hull, valve and towing rope.
