Basket, burner, ballast packages, hull, net and towing rope.
Basket, basket ring, Valve, net, hull and towing rope.
Burner, ballast packages, instruments, net and towing rope.
q.e: The Empty Mass (basic empty mass) of a gas balloon includes the fixed structural components: basket, basket ring (load ring), valve, net, hull (envelope), and towing rope. It does not include consumables like ballast, or items added for specific flights like extra instruments. This is the reference for calculating useful load.

q.t: Before take-off, the balloon pilot realises that the maximum take-off mass has been exceeded by 5%. What has to be done?
o: The load has to be reduced to maximum take-off mass.
During take-off, special care has to be taken for obstacles.
With exceeding up to 5%, normal take-off can be performed.
Take-off has to be approved by the airfield manager on duty.
q.e: Maximum take-off mass limitations must never be exceeded under any circumstances. If the maximum take-off mass has been exceeded (even by 5%), payload must be reduced to at or below the maximum before flight. Operating above maximum mass is illegal and unsafe — performance, structural limits, and lift calculations are all based on the certified maximum.

q.t: Information about operational limits, loading and performance about an aircraft can be taken from which document?
q.e: The Operating Handbook (or Flight Manual) is the primary reference for operational limitations, weight and balance, performance data, normal and emergency procedures. It is a mandatory document that must be on board the aircraft and is specific to that balloon type.

q.t: What effect has air temperature on the carrying force and on maximum take-off mass of a balloon?
o: Maximum take-off mass is higher at low temperatures.
Maximum take-off mass is lower at low temperatures.
Carrying force is higher at low temperatures.
Carrying force is lower at low temperatures.
q.e: Lower air temperature means higher air density (denser air = more mass per cubic metre). Higher air density increases the aerostatic lift (carrying force) since buoyancy = air density × volume × g. Therefore, on cold days, balloons have greater lift and can carry more payload — maximum take-off mass is higher in cold conditions.

q.t: What effect has the elevation above MSL of an airfield on the carrying force and maximum take-off mass of a balloon?
o: The higher the elevation, the lower the carrying force.
The lower the elevation, the lower the maximum take-off mass.
The lower the elevation, the higher the maximum take-off mass.
The higher the elevation, the greater the carrying force.
q.e: Higher elevation means lower atmospheric pressure and lower air density. Aerostatic lift = air density × volume × g. Lower air density means less buoyancy, so carrying force decreases with increasing elevation. Higher altitudes also mean reduced performance — the balloon can carry less payload.

q.t: What difference will be experienced during take-off in presence of a strong surface inversion, compared to a take-off with decreasing temperature with height?
o: During climb through an inversion, less ballast must be released and/or less heating is required.
During climb through an inversion, less ballast must be released and/or more heating is required.
During climb through an inversion, more ballast must be released and/or more heating is required.
During climb through an inversion, more ballast must be released and/or less heating is required.
q.e: In a strong surface inversion, temperature increases with altitude. As the balloon climbs through the inversion, it encounters increasingly warmer (denser) air. The increased air density above increases buoyancy and the balloon requires more effort to maintain altitude (or descend) — actually the balloon may slow its climb. For a gas balloon needing to climb through an inversion, more ballast must be dropped or (for hot air) more heating applied.

q.t: What has to be expected when diving into an inversion layer from above?
q.e: When a balloon descends into an inversion layer from above, it enters increasingly denser (cooler) air below the inversion. The higher-density air below provides more buoyancy, reducing the rate of descent. The balloon effectively 'floats' into the denser air layer, which cushions the descent. This can result in a sudden slowing or cessation of descent.

q.t: Given masses: Empty 240kg, Instruments 20kg, per gas container 30kg, per person 80kg. Up to which pressure altitude can the balloon climb with 5 persons and 4 gas containers, at temperatures 10° below ISA? (use attachment ECQB-PPL_BPL001)
q.e: Total mass = 240 + 20 + (4 × 30) + (5 × 80) = 240 + 20 + 120 + 400 = 780 kg. At ISA-10 conditions, from the chart (ECQB-PPL_BPL001), with a total mass of 780 kg and ISA-10 temperature line, the intersection with the pressure altitude lines gives approximately 13,000 ft as the maximum ceiling.

q.t: Given masses: Empty 260kg, Instruments 20kg, per gas container 30kg, per person 80kg. At ISA+10, how many persons may be carried at max, if balloon with 4 gas containers has to climb to 12,000 ft pressure altitude?
q.e: From the chart at 12,000 ft and ISA+10, the maximum carrying capacity is read. Fixed mass = 260 + 20 + (4 × 30) = 400 kg. From chart at ISA+10 / 12,000 ft, max total mass ≈ 640 kg. Available for persons = 640 - 400 = 240 kg. Persons = 240 ÷ 80 = 3 persons.

q.t: Given masses: Empty 260kg, Instruments 20kg, per gas container 30kg, per person 80kg. At ISA, how many persons may be carried at max, if balloon with 4 gas containers has to climb to 9,000 ft?
q.e: Fixed mass = 260 + 20 + (4 × 30) = 400 kg. From chart at ISA / 9,000 ft, maximum carrying capacity ≈ 720 kg. Available for persons = 720 - 400 = 320 kg. Persons = 320 ÷ 80 = 4 persons maximum.

q.t: What effect has the elevation above MSL of an airfield on the carrying force and maximum take-off mass of a balloon? (repeated)
o: The lower the elevation, the lower the maximum take-off mass.
The lower the elevation, the greater the carrying force.
The lower the elevation, the higher the maximum take-off mass.
The higher the elevation, the greater the carrying force.
q.e: Lower elevation means higher air pressure and higher air density. Greater air density produces more aerostatic lift (buoyancy), allowing a higher maximum take-off mass. Conversely, high elevation aerodromes have lower air density, less lift, and reduced payload capacity. Performance always improves at lower elevation.

q.t: What is the purpose of 'interception lines' in visual navigation?
o: They are used as easily recognizable guidance upon a possible loss of orientation
To visualize the range limitation from the departure aerodrome
They help to continue the flight when flight visibility drops below VFR minima
To mark the next available en-route airport during the flight
q.e: Interception lines (also called line features or catching features) are prominent linear landmarks — motorways, railways, rivers, coastlines — planned perpendicular to or at an angle to the flight path. If the pilot becomes uncertain of position, they fly to the interception line and follow it to a known point, regaining orientation.

q.t: The upper limit of LO R 16 equals... (PFP-056)
q.e: From chart PFP-056, LO R 16 shows '1500 FT MSL' as the lower limit (GND) and 'FL150' as the upper limit. Restricted areas are defined by lower and upper limits; the 'LO R' designation indicates a low-level restricted area, but its upper limit as shown on the chart is FL150.

q.t: The upper limit of LO R 4 equals... (PFP-030)
q.e: From chart PFP-030, LO R 4 shows an upper limit of 4,500 ft MSL. The chart legend shows '4500 FT MSL' as the ceiling of this restricted area. Reading ICAO aeronautical charts correctly requires distinguishing between MSL (altitude) and AGL (height) references.

q.t: Up to which altitude is an overflight prohibited according to the NOTAM? (PFP-024)
q.e: From the NOTAM text: 'Q) EDWW/QROLP/... /000/095/...' — the Q line shows the upper limit as 095 (= FL095 = 9500 ft in NOTAM Q field format). Field G states '9500 FT AMSL' — overflight is prohibited up to 9500 ft MSL (altitude). AMSL = Above Mean Sea Level = MSL altitude.

q.t: What must be considered for cross-border flights?
q.e: Cross-border flights require a flight plan to be filed. International flights (crossing national borders) must have a flight plan submitted to ATC/FIS, meeting ICAO and national requirements. This allows tracking across FIR boundaries and coordination between different states' ATC systems.

q.t: During a flight, a flight plan can be filed at the...
q.e: During a flight, a flight plan can be filed or modified by contacting the Flight Information Service (FIS) on the appropriate frequency. FIS can relay the flight plan information to the relevant authorities. AIS handles pre-flight aeronautical information; SAR handles emergencies.

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a group of unlighted obstacles? (PFP-061)
q.e: From PFP-061 (ICAO chart symbols for obstacles): Symbol C shows a group of unlighted obstacles (multiple obstacle triangles without illumination indicators). Symbol A shows a single lighted obstacle; B shows a group of lighted obstacles; D shows a single unlighted obstacle.

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a civil airport (not international airport) with paved runway? (PFP-062)
q.e: From PFP-062 (ICAO airport symbols): Symbol B represents a civil aerodrome with a paved runway (hard surface) that is not an international airport — shown as a circle with a line through it. International airports use a different symbol. The filled/coloured variants indicate lighting.

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a general spot elevation? (PFP-063)
q.e: From PFP-063 (ICAO chart symbols for elevations): Symbol C shows a general spot elevation — a dot with the elevation figure in plain text. Symbol D shows a controlled spot elevation (in a box); A and B show different types of highest points or benchmarks. Spot elevations in plain text are general reference elevations.

q.t: The majority of aviation accidents are caused by...
q.e: Studies consistently show that around 70-80% of aviation accidents involve human factors as the primary cause. This includes pilot error, crew resource management failures, maintenance errors, and ATC errors. Technical failures account for a much smaller proportion.

q.t: The 'swiss cheese model' can be used to explain the...
o: state of readiness of a pilot.
q.e: James Reason's Swiss Cheese Model illustrates how accidents occur when multiple defensive barriers (represented as slices of Swiss cheese) each have holes (weaknesses), and when the holes align, a hazard passes through all defences causing an accident. It models the error chain concept.

q.t: What is the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere at 6000 ft?
q.e: The percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere remains approximately 21% regardless of altitude (up to about 80 km). What changes with altitude is the partial pressure of oxygen — it decreases as total atmospheric pressure decreases, causing hypoxia at higher altitudes.

q.t: What is the percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere?
q.e: Nitrogen makes up approximately 78% of the atmosphere. Oxygen accounts for about 21%, and the remaining 1% consists of argon, carbon dioxide, and other trace gases. These proportions remain constant throughout the lower atmosphere.

q.t: At which altitude is the atmospheric pressure approximately half the MSL value (1013 hPa)?
q.e: Atmospheric pressure halves approximately every 18,000 ft (roughly 5,500 m). Therefore at 18,000 ft (~FL180), pressure is approximately 506 hPa — about half of the MSL standard pressure of 1013.25 hPa. This is a key threshold for oxygen requirements.

q.t: Air consists of oxygen, nitrogen and other gases. What is the approximate percentage of other gases?
q.e: The atmosphere is composed of approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and about 1% other gases (mainly argon at ~0.93%, plus carbon dioxide, neon, helium, and other trace gases). This composition is constant in the lower atmosphere.

q.t: Carbon monoxide poisoning can be caused by...
q.e: Smoking is a significant source of carbon monoxide (CO) exposure. CO binds to haemoglobin with 200-250 times greater affinity than oxygen, reducing the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. This is particularly dangerous at altitude where oxygen partial pressure is already reduced.

q.t: Which of the following symptoms may indicate hypoxia?
o: Blue marks all over the body
Blue discolouration of lips and fingernails
Muscle cramps in the upper body area
Joint pain in knees and feet
q.e: Cyanosis — blue discolouration of lips, fingernails, and skin — is a classic visible symptom of hypoxia, caused by deoxygenated haemoglobin in the blood. Other symptoms include euphoria, impaired judgement, headache, and eventual loss of consciousness.

q.t: Which of the human senses is most influenced by hypoxia?
q.e: Vision is the most sensitive sense to hypoxia. Night vision (scotopic vision) is significantly impaired even at relatively low altitudes (around 5000 ft at night) because the rod cells in the retina are highly oxygen-dependent. Visual acuity and colour perception also deteriorate.

q.t: From which altitude on does the body usually react to the decreasing atmospheric pressure?
q.e: The body begins to show physiological reactions to reduced atmospheric pressure (and thus reduced oxygen partial pressure) from around 7000 ft, particularly in terms of night vision degradation. Below this altitude, the body can generally compensate adequately.

q.t: Which altitude marks the lower limit where the body is unable to completely compensate the effects of the low atmospheric pressure?
q.e: Above approximately 12,000 ft (3,700 m), the body can no longer fully compensate for the reduced oxygen partial pressure. Supplemental oxygen becomes increasingly important above this altitude. FAA regulations require oxygen use above 12,500 ft for extended periods.

q.t: What is the function of the red blood cells (erythrocytes)?
q.e: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and transports it to body tissues. Immune defence is the role of white blood cells, blood sugar regulation is performed by the pancreas/liver, and coagulation involves platelets and clotting factors.

q.t: Which characteristic is important when choosing sunglasses used by pilots?
q.e: Pilots must use non-polarised sunglasses because polarised lenses can interfere with the visibility of LCD cockpit displays, make certain weather phenomena (like ice crystals or water glare useful for horizon detection) harder to see, and can affect perception of other surfaces.

q.t: In which situation is it NOT possible to achieve a pressure compensation between the middle ear and the environment?
o: During a light and slow climb
Breathing takes place using the mouth only
q.e: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, allowing pressure equalisation. When it is blocked (e.g., due to a cold or upper respiratory infection), pressure equalisation cannot occur during altitude changes, causing barotrauma (ear pain and potential injury). Pilots should not fly with a blocked Eustachian tube.

q.t: Visual illusions are mostly caused by...
q.e: Visual illusions in aviation arise because the brain misinterprets sensory information. The brain relies on previous experience and expectations to interpret visual data; when the environment is unusual (e.g., featureless terrain, night, IMC), it can create misleading perceptions.

q.t: The average decrease of blood alcohol level for an adult in one hour is approximately...
q.e: The average rate of alcohol metabolism in adults is approximately 0.1 per mille (0.1‰) per hour, or 0.01% BAC per hour. This is variable by individual, but is the standard reference value. This means alcohol takes many hours to clear — relevant for pilots needing to comply with minimum 'bottle to throttle' periods.

q.t: A risk factor for decompression sickness is...
q.e: Scuba diving causes dissolved nitrogen in body tissues (from breathing compressed air under pressure). If a pilot flies too soon after diving, the reduced cabin pressure can cause dissolved nitrogen to form bubbles in tissues, causing decompression sickness (the 'bends'). Minimum wait times must be observed.

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the short-term memory?
o: It can store 5 (±2) items for 1 to 2 minutes
It can store 3 (±1) items for 5 to 10 seconds
It can store 7 (±2) items for 10 to 20 seconds
It can store 10 (±5) items for 30 to 60 seconds
q.e: Short-term (working) memory can hold approximately 7 ± 2 items (Miller's Law) for about 10-20 seconds without rehearsal. This has direct implications for ATC readbacks and cockpit task management — information not processed or written down quickly may be lost.

q.t: For what approximate time period can the short-time memory store information?
q.e: Short-term memory retains information for approximately 10 to 20 seconds without active rehearsal or mental repetition. This is why readbacks in aviation are critical — the short window means ATC instructions must be immediately confirmed and/or written down.

q.t: What is a latent error?
o: An error which has an immediate effect on the controls
An error which is made by the pilot actively and consciously
An error which remains undetected in the system for a long time
An error which only has consequences after landing
q.e: A latent error (or latent condition) is one that exists within a system undetected for a long time, often originating from management decisions, design flaws, or training inadequacies. It contrasts with active errors that have immediate consequences. Latent errors are key elements of Reason's accident causation model.

q.t: The ongoing process to monitor the current flight situation is called...
q.e: Situational Awareness (SA) is the continuous perception, comprehension, and projection of the current state of the flight environment — including aircraft position, weather, traffic, system status, and time. Loss of SA is a major contributing factor in aviation accidents.

q.t: Regarding the communication model, how can the use of the same code during radio communication be ensured?
o: By the use of proper headsets
By the use of radio phraseology
By using radios certified for aviation use only
q.e: Standard ICAO radio phraseology ensures that both sender and receiver use the same 'code' (shared language and terminology), minimising misunderstanding. Aviation phraseology reduces ambiguity — a critical safety measure given the consequences of miscommunication in the cockpit.

q.t: In what different ways can a risk be handled appropriately?
q.e: Standard risk management offers four strategies: Avoid (eliminate the risk entirely), Reduce (mitigate the probability or impact), Transfer (shift the risk to another party, e.g., insurance), and Accept (acknowledge and proceed with awareness). 'Ignore' is never a valid risk management strategy.

q.t: Under which circumstances is it more likely to accept higher risks?
o: During check flights due to a high level of nervousness
During flight planning when excellent weather is forecast
If there is not enough information available
q.e: Group dynamics — such as peer pressure, groupthink, authority gradients, and the desire to conform — can lead individuals to accept higher risks than they would alone. This is particularly relevant in crew environments where speaking up against a more senior pilot may feel uncomfortable.

q.t: Which dangerous attitudes are often combined?
q.e: The 'macho' attitude (feeling the need to prove oneself, taking unnecessary risks) and 'invulnerability' (believing accidents happen to others, not oneself) frequently occur together. Both attitudes lead to risk underestimation and are addressed specifically in CRM/HFACS training.

q.t: What is an indication for a macho attitude?
o: Quick resignation in complex and critical situations
Comprehensive risk assessment when faced with unfamiliar situations
Risky flight maneuvers to impress spectators on ground
q.e: A 'macho' dangerous attitude involves taking unnecessary risks to impress others or prove one's abilities. Performing risky manoeuvres to impress spectators is a classic example. This attitude dismisses proper risk management in favour of showing off.

q.t: Which factor can lead to human error?
o: To be doubtful if something looks unclear or ambiguous
The bias to see what we expect to see
q.e: Confirmation bias — the tendency to see what we expect to see — is a major source of human error. Pilots may misread an instrument, assume a clearance was given, or overlook a warning because their brain 'fills in' expected information. Double-checks and checklists help counteract this bias.

q.t: What is the best combination of traits with respect to the individual attitude and behaviour for a pilot?
q.e: Research in aviation psychology suggests that extroverted and emotionally stable personalities tend to perform best as pilots. Extroversion supports communication and teamwork, while emotional stability (low neuroticism) supports performance under pressure and rational decision-making.

q.t: The ideal level of arousal is at which point in the diagram? (HPL-002, P=Performance, A=Arousal)
q.e: The Yerkes-Dodson curve shows that performance peaks at an optimal (moderate) level of arousal — Point C in the diagram represents this peak. Too little arousal (A) leads to boredom/inattentiveness; too much (D) leads to overload and degraded performance.

q.t: At which point in the diagram will a pilot find himself to be overstrained? (HPL-002)
q.e: Point D on the Yerkes-Dodson curve represents excessive arousal/stress, where performance has degraded significantly from the peak. At this level, a pilot is overstrained — stress and anxiety are so high that decision-making, attention, and motor skills are all impaired.

q.t: Which of the following qualities are influenced by stress? (1. Attention 2. Concentration 3. Responsiveness 4. Memory)
q.e: Stress affects all cognitive functions: attention (narrowing of focus), concentration (harder to sustain), responsiveness (reaction times change), and memory (both encoding new information and retrieving stored information are impaired). This is why stress management is a core component of CRM training.

q.t: What clouds and weather may result from an humid and instable air mass, that is pushed against a chain of mountains by the predominant wind and forced to rise?
o: Embedded CB with thunderstorms and showers of hail and/or rain.
Overcast low stratus (high fog) with no precipitation.
Smooth, unstructured NS cloud with light drizzle or snow.
Thin Altostratus and Cirrostratus clouds with light and steady precipitation.
q.e: When unstable, humid air is forced to rise over mountains (orographic lifting), it triggers deep convective development. In unstable conditions, cumulus clouds grow rapidly into cumulonimbus (CB) with associated thunderstorms, hail, and heavy showers.

q.t: What type of fog emerges if humid and almost saturated air, is forced to rise upslope of hills or shallow mountains by the prevailing wind?
q.e: Orographic fog (hill fog) forms when moist air is forced to rise along hillsides or shallow mountains. As it rises, it cools to its dew point and condensation occurs, forming fog or low cloud on the windward slopes.

q.t: What is the gas composition of "air"?
o: Oxygen 21%, Water vapour 78%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
Nitrogen 21%, Oxygen 78%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
Oxygen 21%, Nitrogen 78%, Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1%
q.e: Dry air is composed of approximately 78% nitrogen (N₂), 21% oxygen (O₂), and about 1% other gases (mainly argon, plus CO₂ and trace gases).

q.t: Weather phenomena are most common to be found in which atmospheric layer?
q.e: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere (0-11 km in ISA), containing about 75% of the atmosphere's mass and virtually all water vapour. Nearly all weather phenomena occur here.

q.t: What is the mass of a "cube of air" with the edges 1 m long, at MSL according ISA?
q.e: According to the ICAO Standard Atmosphere (ISA), standard air density at Mean Sea Level is 1.225 kg/m³. Therefore a cubic metre of air weighs exactly 1.225 kg.

q.t: At what rate does the temperature change with increasing height according to ISA (ICAO Standard Atmosphere) within the troposphere?
q.e: The ISA standard temperature lapse rate in the troposphere is a steady decrease of approximately 2°C per 1000 ft (or exactly 6.5°C per 1000 m / 0.65°C per 100 m).

q.t: What is the mean height of the tropopause according to ISA (ICAO Standard Atmosphere)?
q.e: The tropopause in the ICAO Standard Atmosphere is defined at a standard altitude of 11,000 meters (approximately 36,089 ft).

q.t: The term "tropopause" is defined as...
o: the layer above the troposphere showing an increasing temperature.
the height above which the temperature starts to decrease.
the boundary area between the mesosphere and the stratosphere.
the boundary area between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
q.e: The tropopause is the transition boundary zone between the weather-active troposphere below and the stable stratosphere above.

q.t: Temperatures will be given by meteorological aviation services in Europe in which unit?
q.e: European aviation meteorological services (METARs, TAFs) report temperatures in degrees Celsius (°C) in accordance with ICAO and EASA regional standards.

q.t: What is meant by "inversion layer"?
o: An atmospheric layer where temperature increases with increasing height
A boundary area between two other layers within the atmosphere
An atmospheric layer with constant temperature with increasing height
An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases with increasing height
q.e: An inversion layer is an anomaly where temperature increases with altitude, "inverting" the normal lapse rate. This traps air and prevents convection.

q.t: What is meant by "isothermal layer"?
o: A boundary area between two other layers within the atmosphere
An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases with increasing height
An atmospheric layer where temperature increases with increasing height
An atmospheric layer with constant temperature with increasing height
q.e: An isothermal layer maintains a constant temperature as altitude increases. The lower stratosphere is a classic example of an isothermal layer.

q.t: The temperature lapse rate with increasing height within the troposphere according ISA is...
q.e: The formal ISA standard environmental lapse rate is exactly 0.65°C per 100 meters (which translates to roughly 2°C per 1,000 feet).

q.t: Which process may result in an inversion layer at about 5000 ft (1500 m) height?
o: Intensive sunlight insolation during a warm summer day
Ground cooling by radiation during the night
Advection of cool air in the upper troposphere
Widespread descending air within a high pressure area
q.e: Subsidence inversions form when a broad layer of air sinks (subsides) in a high-pressure system, compressing and warming as it descends, often settling around 5,000 ft.

q.t: An inversion layer close to the ground can be caused by...
o: thickening of clouds in medium layers.
q.e: Radiation inversions form near the ground at night when the surface cools rapidly by emitting infrared radiation, cooling the air immediately above it.

q.t: What is the ISA standard pressure at FL 180 (5500 m)?
q.e: At FL180 (approximately 18,000 ft or 5,500 m), atmospheric pressure is halved compared to MSL, making it approximately 500 hPa.

q.t: Which processes result in decreasing air density?
q.e: Air density decreases when it expands due to heat (increasing temperature) or when the ambient pressure pushing the molecules together drops (decreasing pressure).

q.t: The pressure at MSL in ISA conditions is...
q.e: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere precisely defines Mean Sea Level (MSL) pressure as 1013.25 hPa (equivalent to 29.92 inHg).

q.t: The barometric altimeter indicates height above...
q.e: A barometric altimeter mechanically measures the difference between ambient pressure and the specific reference pressure dialed into its subscale window (QNH, QFE, or QNE).

q.t: The altimeter can be checked on the ground by setting...
o: QNE and checking that the indication shows zero on the ground.
QFF and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QNH and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QFE and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
q.e: By setting the local QNH on the ground, the altimeter should read the official elevation of the airfield. This is the standard pre-flight altimeter check.

q.t: The barometric altimeter with QNH setting indicates...
o: height above the pressure level at airfield elevation.
q.e: QNH is the pressure setting that provides indicated altitude (height above Mean Sea Level). It is not "true" altitude unless temperatures are exactly ISA standard.

q.t: How can wind speed and wind direction be derived from surface weather charts?
o: By annotations from the text part of the chart
By alignment of lines of warm- and cold fronts.
By alignment and distance of isobaric lines
By alignment and distance of hypsometric lines
q.e: Isobars (lines of equal pressure) show wind direction (parallel to the lines) and wind speed (closer lines mean a stronger pressure gradient and faster winds).

q.t: Which force causes "wind"?
q.e: The fundamental driver of all wind is the Pressure Gradient Force — air accelerating from an area of high pressure toward an area of low pressure.

q.t: Above the friction layer, with a prevailing pressure gradient, the wind direction is...
o: at an angle of 30° to the isobars towards low pressure.
q.e: Above the friction layer, the Coriolis force turns the wind until it balances the pressure gradient force, resulting in "geostrophic wind" that blows parallel to the isobars.

q.t: Which of the stated surfaces will reduce the wind speed most due to ground friction?
o: Flat land, lots of vegetation cover
Flat land, deserted land, no vegetation
q.e: Friction is determined by surface roughness. Mountainous terrain covered in vegetation presents the highest physical resistance, reducing wind speed the most at ground level.

q.t: The movement of air flowing together is called...
q.e: Convergence is the meteorological term for air masses flowing together horizontally, which subsequently forces the air to rise.

q.t: The movement of air flowing apart is called...
q.e: Divergence describes air spreading out horizontally away from a central region. At the surface, it is typically associated with high-pressure systems and descending air.

q.t: What weather development will result from convergence at ground level?
q.e: When air converges at the surface, it has nowhere to go but up. This ascending air cools, moisture condenses, and clouds form.

q.t: When air masses meet each other head on, how is this referred to and what air movements will follow?
o: Divergence resulting in air being lifted
Convergence resulting in air being lifted
q.e: Meeting head-on is called convergence. Because the air cannot go into the ground, it is forced upward (lifted), creating clouds and precipitation.

q.t: What are the air masses that Central Europe is mainly influenced by?
o: Polar cold air and tropical warm air
q.e: Central Europe sits in the mid-latitudes, acting as the primary battleground between cold Polar air from the north and warm Tropical air from the south.

q.t: With regard to global circulation within the atmosphere, where does polar cold air meets subtropical warm air?
o: At the subtropical high pressure belt
q.e: The polar front is the continuous, dynamic boundary in the mid-latitudes where cold polar air clashes with warmer subtropical air, spawning frontal low-pressure systems.

q.t: Foehn conditions usually develop with...
o: instability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
stability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
stability, high pressure area with calm wind.
instability, high pressure area with calm wind.
q.e: Foehn winds develop when a stable, widespread air mass is forced over a mountain ridge, losing moisture on the way up and warming dynamically on the way down.

q.t: What type of turbulence is typically found close to the ground on the lee side during Foehn conditions?
q.e: Rotor turbulence forms at the surface underneath mountain waves on the lee side of a range during Foehn conditions. It is notoriously violent and dangerous.

q.t: Light turbulence always has to be expected...
o: above cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
below cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
below stratiform clouds in medium layers.
q.e: Thermals (rising columns of warm air) generate cumulus clouds. Flying below these clouds means flying through the active, bumpy convective currents feeding them.

q.t: Moderate to severe turbulence has to be expected...
o: on the lee side of a mountain range when rotor clouds are present.
below thick cloud layers on the windward side of a mountain range.
with the appearance of extended low stratus clouds (high fog).
q.e: Rotor clouds mark areas of severe mechanical turbulence and violent updrafts/downdrafts caused by mountain waves on the lee side of a range.

q.t: Which answer contains every state of water found in the atmosphere?
q.e: Water exists simultaneously in the atmosphere as a gas (invisible water vapour), a liquid (rain, cloud droplets), and a solid (snow, hail, ice crystals).

q.t: How do dew point and relative humidity change with decreasing temperature?
o: Dew point increases, relative humidity decreases
Dew point remains constant, relative humidity decreases
Dew point remains constant, relative humidity increases
Dew point decreases, relative humidity increases
q.e: If temperature drops but the actual moisture content remains the same, the dew point is constant, but the air approaches saturation, so relative humidity increases.

q.t: How do spread and relative humidity change with increasing temperature?
o: Spread remains constant, relative humidity increases
Spread remains constant, relative humidity decreases
q.e: As temperature increases, the capacity of the air to hold water grows. The spread (gap between temp and dew point) widens, and relative humidity decreases.

q.t: The "spread" is defined as...
o: difference between dew point and condensation point.
relation of actual to maximum possible humidity of air.
difference between actual temperature and dew point.
maximum amount of water vapour that can be contained in air.
q.e: The temperature-dew point spread is the physical difference (in degrees) between the current air temperature and the dew point. A small spread warns of fog or clouds.

q.t: With other factors remaining constant, decreasing temperature results in...
o: decreasing spread and decreasing relative humidity.
decreasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
increasing spread and decreasing relative humidity.
increasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
q.e: Cooling the air brings the temperature closer to the dew point (decreasing the spread). As the spread shrinks, the air approaches 100% saturation (increasing relative humidity).

q.t: What process causes latent heat being released into the upper troposphere?
q.e: Latent heat is absorbed during evaporation and released during condensation. When clouds form, the gas-to-liquid transition releases heat, which fuels further storm development.

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate is...
o: proportional to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
higher than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
lower than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
equal to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
q.e: Because condensing water releases latent heat, a rising parcel of saturated air cools slower (approx. 1.5°C/1000 ft) than dry air (3°C/1000 ft).

q.t: The dry adiabatic lapse rate has a value of...
q.e: The Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR) is fixed by physical laws at 1.0°C per 100 meters (or approximately 3°C per 1,000 feet).

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate should be assumed with a mean value of:
q.e: While it varies with temperature and pressure, standard meteorological calculations use a mean Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR) of 0.6°C per 100 meters.

q.t: What weather conditions may be expected during conditionally unstable conditions?
o: Towering cumulus, isolated showers of rain or thunderstorms
Layered clouds up to high levels, prolonged rain or snow
Shallow cumulus clouds with base at medium levels
Sky clear of clouds, sunshine, low winds
q.e: Conditional instability means the air is stable if dry, but unstable if saturated. If lifted to saturation, it erupts into deep convection (towering cumulus, Cb, showers).

q.t: Which conditions are likely for the formation of advection fog?
o: Cold, humid air moves over a warm ocean
Humidity evaporates from warm, humid ground into cold air
Warm, humid air cools during a cloudy night
Warm, humid air moves over a cold surface
q.e: Advection fog forms when moist, relatively warm air is blown horizontally (advected) over a cooler surface, chilling the air from below until it saturates.

q.t: Clouds are basically distinguished by what types?
q.e: Meteorologically, all clouds fall into two main families based on air stability: Cumuliform (heaped, convective, unstable) and Stratiform (layered, stable).

q.t: Clouds in high layers are referred to as...
q.e: The prefix "Cirro-" (meaning "curl of hair") denotes high-altitude ice clouds. "Alto-" is for medium levels, and "Strato-" is for low, layered clouds.

q.t: What weather phenomenon designated by "2" has to be expected on the lee side during "Foehn" conditions?
q.e: Altocumulus lenticularis (lens-shaped clouds) form in the crests of mountain standing waves. They remain stationary and indicate severe mountain wave turbulence.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show? (MET-002)
q.e: The image shows classic Cumulus clouds — detached, fluffy, cauliflower-like heaps with flat bases, indicating fair-weather thermal convection.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show? (MET-004)
q.e: The image shows Cirrus clouds — delicate, wispy, fibrous hair-like strands made entirely of ice crystals at very high altitudes.

q.t: What factor may affect the top of cumulus clouds?
o: The presence of an inversion layer
q.e: An inversion layer acts like a physical lid. The warm air in the inversion stops the rising convective currents, preventing cumulus clouds from growing taller.

q.t: What factors may indicate a tendency to fog formation?
q.e: A low temperature-dew point spread means the air is nearly saturated. If the temperature continues to decrease, saturation is reached, and fog will form.

q.t: What condition may prevent the formation of "radiation fog"?
q.e: Overcast clouds act like a thermal blanket, absorbing and radiating heat back to the ground. This prevents the surface from cooling enough to form radiation fog.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "advection fog"?
o: Warm, moist air is moved across cold ground areas
Cold, moist air is being moved across warm ground areas
Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
q.e: Advection fog is literally "moving" fog. It requires wind to push a warm, humid air mass over a cold surface (land or sea), which chills the air to its dew point.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "orographic fog" ("hill fog")?
o: Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Warm, moist air is moved across a hill or a mountain range
Evaporation from warm, moist ground area into very cold air
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
q.e: As wind blows moist air against a mountain, the air is forced upward. It expands and cools adiabatically until it condenses into "hill fog" on the slopes.

q.t: What factors are required for the formation of precipitation in clouds?
o: The presence of an inversion layer
Calm winds and intensive sunlight insolation
q.e: Updrafts keep tiny water droplets suspended in the cloud. They bounce around, collide, and merge (coalesce) until they are heavy enough to fall as precipitation.

q.t: The formation of medium to large precipitation particles requires...
q.e: Strong updrafts (like those in towering cumulus or Cb) hold droplets aloft much longer, allowing them to collect more water or ice before eventually falling.

q.t: Which type of cloud is associated with prolonged rain?
q.e: Nimbostratus ("nimbo" = rain, "strato" = layer) is a thick, dark, widespread cloud layer that blocks out the sun and delivers continuous, prolonged precipitation.

q.t: Regarding the type of cloud, precipitation is classified as...
q.e: Precipitation is classified by its source: Stratiform clouds produce steady, continuous "rain" or "snow", while cumuliform clouds produce intermittent "showers".

q.t: How is an air mass described when moving to Central Europe via the Russian continent during winter?
q.e: Air originating over the vast, cold landmass of Russia in winter is dry (Continental) and cold (Polar), leading to clear, freezing weather in Central Europe.

q.t: The character of an air mass is given by what properties?
o: Temperatures at origin and present region
Region of origin and track during movement
q.e: An air mass inherits its baseline properties (temperature/humidity) from its source region, and it is modified by the surface it tracks over as it moves.

q.t: The symbol labeled (1) as shown in the picture is a / an...
q.e: A solid blue line with triangles pointing in the direction of movement is the international meteorological symbol for a cold front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (2) as shown in the picture is a / an...
q.e: A solid red line with semi-circles pointing in the direction of movement is the standard symbol for a warm front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (3) as shown in the picture is a / an...
q.e: A purple or magenta line with alternating triangles and semi-circles represents an occluded front, where a cold front has caught up to a warm front.

q.t: What cloud sequence can typically be observed during the passage of a warm front?
o: Squall lines with showers of rain and thunderstorms (Cb), gusting wind followed by cumulus clouds with isolated showers of rain
Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds and warming during summer; formation of extended high fog layers during winter
Cirrus, thickening altostratus and altocumulus clouds, lowering cloud base with rain, nimbostratus
In coastal areas during daytime wind from the coast and forming of cumulus clouds, dissipation of clouds during evening and night
q.e: A warm front approaches gradually, showing high Cirrus first, which thickens and lowers into Altostratus, finally becoming Nimbostratus with steady rain.

q.t: What clouds and weather can typically be observed during the passage of a cold front?
o: Strongly developed cumulus clouds (Cb) with showers of rain and thunderstorms, gusting wind followed by cumulus clouds with isolated showers of rain
Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds and warming during summer; formation of extended high fog layers during winter
Cirrus, thickening altostratus and altocumulus clouds, lowering cloud base with rain, nimbostratus
In coastal areas during daytime wind from the coast and forming of cumulus clouds, dissipation of clouds during evening and night
q.e: Cold fronts act like a wedge, violently shoving warm air upward. This causes massive instability, generating Cumulonimbus (Cb), thunderstorms, and heavy showers.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected within the warm sector of a polar front low during summer time?
o: Visibilty less than 1000 m, cloud-covered ground
Moderate to good visibility, scattered clouds
Moderate visibility, heavy showers and thunderstorms
Good visibility, some isolated high clouds
q.e: The warm sector (the area between the warm front and the trailing cold front) generally features warm, humid air with scattered fair-weather cumulus and moderate visibility.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected after the passage of a cold front?
o: Poor visibility, formation of overcast or ground-covering stratus clouds, snow
Medium visibility with lowering cloud bases, onset of prolonged precipitation
Good visiblity, formation of cumulus clouds with showers of rain or snow
Scattered cloud layers, visbility more than 5 km, formation of shallow cumulus clouds
q.e: Behind a cold front, the air is cold and unstable but generally clear. Passing over warmer ground triggers scattered cumulus and isolated showers, but visibility is typically excellent.

q.t: A boundary between a cold polar air mass and a warm subtropical air mass showing no horizontal displacement is called...
q.e: When two contrasting air masses meet but neither is strong enough to push the other, the boundary stalls and is termed a stationary front.

q.t: What is the usual direction of movement of a polar front low?
o: To the northeast during winter, to the southeast during summer
Parallel to the the warm-sector isobars
To the northwest during winter, to the southwest during summer
Parallel to the warm front line to the south
q.e: Low pressure systems generally steer in the direction of the upper-level winds, which align closely parallel to the surface isobars found within the system's warm sector.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed during the passage of a polar front low?
o: Falling pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, falling pressure behind the cold front
Falling pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, rising pressure behind the cold front
Rising pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, rising pressure behind the cold front
Rising pressure in front of the warm front, rising pressure within the warm sector, falling pressure behind the cold front
q.e: Pressure falls as the low system approaches, flattens out in the warm sector, and rises sharply once the heavy, dense air of the cold front passes.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed when a cold front is passing?
q.e: The pressure drops to its lowest point right at the frontal boundary. Immediately after the cold front passes, the dense cold air causes pressure to surge upward.

q.t: What change of wind direction can be expected during the passage of a polar front low in Central Europe?
o: Backing wind during passage of the warm front, veering wind during passage of the cold front
Backing wind during passage of the warm front, backing wind during passage of the cold front
Veering wind during passage of the warm front, backing wind during passage of the cold front
Veering wind during passage of the warm front, veering wind during passage of the cold front
q.e: In the Northern Hemisphere, wind always veers (shifts clockwise, e.g., from South to Southwest to Northwest) as frontal boundaries pass over.

q.t: What cloud type can typically be observed across widespread high pressure areas during summer?
q.e: High pressure means subsiding (sinking) air, which suppresses deep cloud development. The result is typically clear skies or isolated, shallow Cumulus clouds.

q.t: What pressure pattern may result from cold-air inflow in high tropospheric layers?
o: Formation of a low in the upper troposphere
Formation of a large ground low
Formation of a high in the upper troposphere
q.e: Cold air is denser and heavier. When it flows into the upper troposphere, it lowers the heights of pressure levels aloft, creating an upper-level low (or trough).

q.t: Cold air inflow in high tropospheric layers may result in...
q.e: Cold air aloft above warm surface air creates a very steep environmental lapse rate. This massive instability fuels deep convection, showers, and thunderstorms.

q.t: What weather phenomena have to be expected around an upper-level trough?
o: Formation of high stratus clouds, ground-covering cloud bases
Calm weather, formation of lifted fog layers
Calm wind, forming of shallow cumulus clouds
q.e: An upper-level trough brings cold air aloft and diverging upper winds, which force upward vertical motion, leading to instability, showers, and thunderstorms.

q.t: What frontal line divides subtropical air from polar cold air, in particular across Central Europe?
q.e: The Polar Front is the semi-permanent, global-scale boundary separating cold polar air masses from warm subtropical air masses.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Changing weather with passing of frontal lines
Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
q.e: Summer high pressure systems feature subsiding air that warms and dries as it sinks. This prevents storm formation, leading to calm, sunny weather with minimal cloud cover.

q.t: What weather conditions in Central Europe are typically found in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Small isobar spacing with strong prevailing northerly winds
Large isobar spacing with calm winds, formation of local wind systems
Large isobar spacing with strong prevailing westerly winds
Small isobar spacing with calm winds, formation of local wind systems
q.e: High pressure means a weak pressure gradient, shown by widely spaced (large) isobars. The resulting calm winds allow local thermal breezes (like mountain or sea breezes) to dominate.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during winter?
o: Changing weather with passing of frontal lines
Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
q.e: Winter highs cause strong surface temperature inversions. Moisture is trapped in the cold, stagnant air near the ground, frequently resulting in widespread, persistent high fog or stratus.

q.t: What wind conditions can be expected in areas showing large distances between isobars?
o: Formation of local wind systems with strong prevailing westerly winds
Strong prevailing westerly winds with rapid veering
Variable winds, formation of local wind systems
Strong prevailing easterly winds with rapid backing
q.e: Large distances between isobars equal a weak pressure gradient force. This results in calm or variable winds, allowing local thermal effects (mountain/valley winds) to take over.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected during "Foehn" on the windward side of a mountain range?
o: Layered clouds, mountains obscured, poor visibility, moderate or heavy rain
Scattered cumulus clouds with showers and thunderstorms
Calm wind and forming of high stratus clouds (high fog)
Dissipating clouds with unusual warming, accompanied by strong, gusty winds
q.e: On the windward (stau) side, moist air is violently forced up the mountain, causing massive condensation, overcast layered clouds, heavy rain/snow, and obscured peaks.

q.t: What situation may result in the occurrence of severe wind shear?
o: When a shower is visible close to the airfield
Cross-country flying below Cu clouds with about 4 octas coverage
During final approach, 30 min after a heavy shower has passed the airfield
Flying ahead of a warm front with visible Ci clouds
q.e: Showers and thunderstorms produce violent, cold downdrafts that hit the ground and spread rapidly outward (gust fronts). Flying near them guarantees severe wind shear.

q.t: What conditions are favourable for the formation of thunderstorms?
o: Warm and dry air, strong inversion layer
Clear night over land, cold air and patches of fog
Calm winds and cold air, overcast cloud cover with St or As.
Warm humid air, conditionally unstable environmental lapse rate
q.e: Thunderstorms require three ingredients: moisture (humid air), instability (an unstable lapse rate), and a lifting mechanism to start the convection.

q.t: What conditions are mandatory for the formation of thermal thunderstorms?
o: Absolutely stable atmosphere, high temperature and high humidity
Absolutely stable atmosphere, high temperature and low humidity
Conditionally unstable atmosphere, high temperature and high humidity
Conditionally unstable atmosphere, low temperature and low humidity
q.e: Thermal thunderstorms form due to intense surface heating. They absolutely require high humidity for storm energy and a conditionally unstable atmosphere to allow the heated air to rise freely.

q.t: With regard to thunderstorms, strong up- and downdrafts appear during the...
q.e: The mature stage is the most violent part of a thunderstorm's lifecycle, characterized by the simultaneous presence of massive updrafts feeding the storm and heavy downdrafts driven by rain.

q.t: Which stage of a thunderstorm is dominated by updrafts?
q.e: The initial or "Cumulus" stage consists entirely of continuous updrafts that build the cloud vertically. No precipitation falls during this stage.

q.t: Heavy downdrafts and strong wind shear close to the ground can be expected...
o: during approach to an airfield at the coast with a strong sea breeze.
during cold, clear nights with the formation of radiation fog.
during warm summer days with high, flatted Cu clouds.
near the rainfall areas of heavy showers or thunderstorms.
q.e: The massive weight of precipitation falling from a Cb pulls cold air down with it. When this downdraft hits the ground, it violently spreads out, causing extreme wind shear.

q.t: What phenomenon is caused by cold air downdrafts with precipitation from a fully developed thunderstorm cloud?
q.e: When a cold downdraft hits the ground and spreads horizontally, its leading edge acts like a mini cold front, known as a gust front, characterized by violent, shifting winds.

q.t: What kind of reduction in visibility is not very sensitive to changes in temperature?
q.e: Haze consists of dry microscopic particles (dust, smoke, pollutants) rather than water droplets. Therefore, unlike fog or mist, it does not evaporate when temperatures rise.

q.t: Information about pressure patterns and frontal situation can be found in which chart?
q.e: Surface weather charts (Synoptic charts) are specifically designed to map out isobars (pressure patterns), Highs, Lows, and frontal boundaries at ground level.

q.t: Which weather chart shows the actual air pressure as in MSL along with pressure centers and fronts?
q.e: The standard surface weather chart maps atmospheric pressure reduced to Mean Sea Level (MSL) using isobars, along with the positions of pressure centers and fronts.

q.t: What information can be obtained from satallite images?
o: Flight visibility, ground visibility, and ground contact
Overview of cloud covers and front lines
Temperature and dew point of environmental air
q.e: Satellites capture images from space, providing a perfect visual overview of cloud coverage, storm systems, and the alignment of major weather fronts.

q.t: What chart shows areas of precipitation?
q.e: Weather radar works by bouncing microwave pulses off water droplets and ice crystals. It is the primary tool for locating and measuring the intensity of precipitation.

q.t: Measured pressure distribution in MSL and corresponding frontal systems are displayed by the...
q.e: Surface weather charts summarize current or forecast weather at the surface, explicitly showing MSL isobars, highs, lows, and frontal lines.

q.t: In a METAR, "heavy rain" is designated by the identifier...
q.e: In METAR coding, the "+" prefix indicates "heavy", and "RA" is the abbreviation for Rain. Thus, +RA means heavy continuous rain.

q.t: In a METAR, "(moderate) showers of rain" are designated by the identifier...
q.e: SH signifies Showers, and "RA" signifies Rain. The absence of a "+" or "-" prefix means it is of moderate intensity.

q.t: An inversion is a layer ...
o: with increasing pressure with increasing height.
with increasing temperature with increasing height.
with constant temperature with increasing height.
with decreasing temperature with increasing height.
q.e: Normally, temperature decreases with height. An inversion is an "inverted" state where a layer of warm air sits above colder air, meaning temperature increases with height.

q.t: What can be expected for the prevailling wind with isobars on a surface weather chart showing large distances?
o: Low pressure gradients resulting in low prevailling wind
Strong pressure gradients resulting in strong prevailling wind
Strong pressure gradients resulting in low prevailling wind
Low pressure gradients resulting in strong prevailling wind
q.e: The distance between isobars indicates pressure gradient. Large distances mean a weak (low) gradient, which results in weak or calm winds.

q.t: What is referred to as mountain wind?
o: Wind blowing uphill from the valley during daytime.
Wind blowing uphill from the valley during the night.
Wind blowing down the mountain side during daytime.
Wind blowing down the mountain side during the night
q.e: At night, mountain slopes cool rapidly. The cold, dense air flows downhill into the valleys under gravity. This nocturnal down-slope flow is the "mountain wind".

q.t: Under which conditions "back side weather" ("Rückseitenwetter") can be expected?
o: During Foehn at the lee side
After passing of a warm front
After passing of a cold front
q.e: Rückseitenwetter (backside weather) describes the cold, unstable, showery, but highly visible air mass that rushes in immediately following a cold front.

q.t: What wind is reportet as 225/15?
q.e: Wind is reported as direction / speed. 225 degrees is Southwest (exactly halfway between South 180° and West 270°). Aviation wind speed is normally reported in knots (kt).

q.t: How does air temperatur change in ISA from MSL to approx. 10.000 m height?
q.e: In the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), MSL temperature is +15°C. Cooling at 6.5°C per 1000m, the temperature at 10,000m is exactly -50°C.

q.t: What weather is likely to be experienced during "Foehn" in the Bavarian area close to the alps?
o: High pressure area overhead Biskaya and low pressure area in Eastern Europe
Nimbostratus cloud in the southern alps, rotor clouds at the lee side, warm and dry wind
Cold, humid downhill wind on the lee side of the alps, flat pressure pattern
Nimbostratus cloud in the northern alps, rotor clouds at the windward side, warm and dry wind
q.e: In a Southern Foehn, the Italian/Austrian side gets heavy rain (Nimbostratus). Bavaria (the lee side) experiences warm, dry, gusty winds falling from the mountains, often with dangerous rotor clouds.

q.t: Mountain side updrafts can be intensified by ...
o: Solar irradiation on the lee side
thermal radiation of the windward side during the night
Solar irradiation on the windward side
By warming of upper atmospheric layers
q.e: When the sun heats the windward side of a mountain, the surface air warms and rises thermally (anabatic wind). This thermal updraft intensifies the mechanical updraft caused by the wind hitting the mountain.

q.t: The rotational axis of the Earth runs through the...
o: geographic North Pole and on the geographic South Pole.
magnetic north pole and on the magnetic south pole.
geographic North Pole and on the magnetic south pole.
magnetic north pole and on the geographic South Pole.
q.e: The Earth rotates around its polar axis, which by definition passes exactly through the geographic North and South Poles.

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the polar axis of the Earth?
o: The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is at an angle of 23.5° to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is at an angle of 66.5° to the plane of the equator
q.e: The geographic polar axis is perfectly perpendicular (90 degrees) to the plane of the geographic equator.

q.t: Which approximate, geometrical form describes the shape of the Earth best for navigation systems?
q.e: For precise navigation (like GPS/WGS-84), the Earth is best modeled as an oblate spheroid or Ellipsoid, because it bulges slightly at the equator. (Note: Often translated poorly in charts as 'Sphere of ecliptical shape', but standard navigation theory uses Ellipsoid).

q.t: The shortest distance between two points on Earth is represented by a part of...
q.e: A great circle represents the intersection of the Earth's surface with a plane passing through the Earth's center, forming the shortest path between any two points.

q.t: The circumference of the Earth at the equator is approximately...
q.e: One degree of latitude equals 60 NM. Since the Earth is 360 degrees around, 360 * 60 = 21,600 NM.

q.t: What is the difference in latitude between A (12°53'30"N) and B (07°34'30"S)?
q.e: Since they are in different hemispheres, you add the latitudes: 12°53'30" + 07°34'30" = 19°87'60" = 20°28'00".

q.t: Where are the two polar circles?
o: north and south of the poles
23.5° north and south of the equator
23.5° north and south of the poles
q.e: The polar circles (Arctic and Antarctic) are located at approximately 66.5° N/S, which is 23.5° from the respective geographic poles.

q.t: What is the distance between the parallels of latitude 48°N and 49°N along a meridian line?
q.e: Along any meridian (longitude line), one degree of latitude equals exactly 60 Nautical Miles.

q.t: What distance corresponds to one degree difference in latitude along any degree of longitude?
q.e: By definition, one minute of latitude equals 1 Nautical Mile. Therefore, one degree (60 minutes) equals 60 NM.

q.t: Point A on the Earth's surface lies exactly on the parallel of latitude of 47°50'27"N. Which point is exactly 240 NM north of A?
q.e: 240 NM north equals 240 minutes of latitude, which is exactly 4 degrees. 47° + 4° = 51°50'27"N.

q.t: What is the distance between the two parallels of longitude 150°E and 151°E along the equator?
q.e: At the equator, the distance between degrees of longitude is at its maximum and equals 60 NM per degree, identical to degrees of latitude.

q.t: What is the great circle distance between two points A and B on the equator when the difference between the two associated meridians is exactly one degree of longitude?
q.e: The equator is a great circle itself, and 1 degree of longitude along the equator spans exactly 60 NM.

q.t: Assume two arbitrary points A and B on the same parallel of latitude, but not on the equator. Point A is located on 010°E and point B on 020°E. The rumb line distance between A and B is always...
q.e: The distance of 10 degrees longitude at the equator is 600 NM. Since parallels of latitude get smaller towards the poles, the distance for 10 degrees will always be less than 600 NM.

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 20° of longitude?
q.e: The Earth rotates 15 degrees per hour. Therefore, 20 degrees takes (20 / 15) = 1.33 hours, which is 1 hour and 20 minutes.

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 10° of longitude?
q.e: The Earth rotates 15 degrees in 60 minutes, which is 4 minutes per degree. 10 degrees * 4 minutes = 40 minutes (0:40 h).

q.t: With Central European Summer Time (CEST) given as UTC+2, what UTC time corresponds to 1600 CEST?
q.e: To find UTC, subtract the offset from local time: 1600 CEST - 2 hours = 1400 UTC.

q.t: UTC is...
o: a local time in Central Europe.
local mean time at a specific point on Earth.
an obligatory time used in aviation.
q.e: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the universal standard time used across all global aviation to prevent timezone confusion.

q.t: With Central European Time (CET) given as UTC+1, what UTC time corresponds to 1700 CET?
q.e: 1700 CET minus the 1 hour offset equals 1600 UTC.

q.t: Vienna (LOWW) is located at 016° 34'E, Salzburg (LOWS) at 013° 00'E. The latitude of both positions can be considered as equal. What is the difference of sunrise and sunset times, expressed in UTC, between Wien and Salzburg?
o: In Vienna the sunrise and sunset are about 4 minutes later than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise and sunset are about 14 minutes earlier than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise is 4 minutes later and sunset is 4 minutes earlier than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise is 14 minutes earlier and sunset is 14 minutes later than in Salzburg
q.e: Vienna is further East by about 3.5 degrees. 3.5 degrees * 4 minutes/degree = 14 minutes. Since it is further East, the sun rises and sets earlier there.

q.t: The term 'civil twilight' is defined as...
o: the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 12 degrees or less below the true horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 6 degrees or less below the apparent horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 6 degrees or less below the true horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 12 degrees or less below the apparent horizon.
q.e: Civil twilight begins/ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the true (ideal) horizon.

q.t: Given: TC: 179°; WCA: -12°; VAR: 004° E; DEV: +002°. What are MH and MC?
The term 'magnetic course' (MC) is defined as...
o: the angle between true north and the course line.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the magnetic north pole.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographic North Pole.
the angle between magnetic north and the course line.
q.e: Magnetic Course is the intended path of the aircraft relative to Magnetic North.

q.t: The term 'True Course' (TC) is defined as...
o: the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographic North Pole.
the angle between true north and the course line.
tthe angle between magnetic north and the course line.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the magnetic north pole.
q.e: True Course is the intended path of the aircraft measured relative to True (Geographic) North.

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are TH and VAR?
q.e: TH = TC + WCA = 183 + 11 = 194°. VAR = TH - MH = 194 - 198 = -4° (which means 4° West).

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are the TH and the DEV?
Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200°. What are the VAR and the DEV?
Where does the inclination reach its lowest value?
q.e: Magnetic inclination (dip) is 0 degrees (lowest value) at the magnetic equator, where the magnetic field lines are perfectly parallel to the Earth's surface.

q.t: The angle between compass north and magnetic north is called...
q.e: Deviation is the error induced in the compass by the aircraft's own local magnetic fields, creating an angle between Magnetic North and Compass North.

q.t: Which direction corresponds to 'compass north' (CN)?
o: The most northerly part of the magnetic compass in the aircraft, where the reading takes place
The direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographical North Pole
The angle between the aircraft heading and magnetic north
The direction to which the direct reading compass aligns due to earth's and aircraft's magnetic fields
q.e: Compass North is the actual direction the needle points, which is a combination of the Earth's magnetic field and local aircraft interference (deviation).

q.t: The term 'isogonal' or 'isogonic line' is defined as a line on an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the same value of...
q.e: Isogonic lines connect points of equal magnetic variation (declination), which helps pilots convert between true and magnetic headings.

q.t: The term 'agonic line' is defined as a line on Earth or an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the...
q.e: An agonic line is a specific isogonic line where the magnetic variation is exactly zero (True North and Magnetic North align perfectly).

q.t: Which are the official basic units for horizontal distances used in aeronautical navigation and their abbreviations?
q.e: Standard ICAO aviation charts use Nautical Miles (NM) for distance, and occasionally kilometers (km) depending on the region or specific VFR chart standard.

q.t: 1000 ft equal...
q.e: One foot is approximately 0.3048 meters. Therefore, 1000 feet is roughly equal to 300 meters.

q.t: 5500 m equal...
q.e: 5500 meters divided by 0.3048 m/ft equals approximately 18,044 feet, heavily rounded to 18,000 feet (FL180, a common pressure transition marker).

q.t: Electronic devices on board of an aeroplane have influence on the...
q.e: Electronic devices emit electromagnetic fields, which interfere directly with the magnetic needle of the direct reading compass, causing deviation.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Mercator chart?
o: The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
q.e: In a Mercator projection, rhumb lines are straight (constant heading), but great circles curve. The scale distorts (increases) significantly as you move toward the poles.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Lambert conformal chart?
o: The chart is conformal and nearly true to scale
Great circles are depicted as straight lines and the chart is an equal-area projection
Rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines and the chart is conformal
The chart is conformal and an equal-area projection
q.e: Lambert Conformal Conic charts are widely used for aviation because a straight line closely approximates a great circle, angles are preserved (conformal), and scale is nearly constant across the map.

q.t: The distance between two airports is 220 NM. On an aeronautical navigation chart the pilot measures 40.7 cm for this distance. The chart scale is...
A distance of 7.5 cm on an aeronautical chart represents a distance of 60.745 NM in reality. What is the chart scale?
An aircraft travels 100 km in 56 minutes. The ground speed (GS) equals...
q.e: Speed = Distance / Time. 100 km / (56 / 60) hours = 107.14 km/h.

q.t: How many satellites are necessary for a precise and verified three-dimensional determination of the position?
q.e: A GPS receiver requires at least 4 satellites to resolve the 4 variables: latitude, longitude, altitude (3D), and time receiver clock error.

q.t: When using a GPS for tracking to the next waypoint, a deviation indication is shown by a vertical bar and dots to the left and to the right of the bar. What statement describes the correct interpretation of the display?
o: The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection is +-10 NM.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection is +-10°
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
q.e: GPS CDI (Course Deviation Indicator) bars show linear cross-track distance (e.g., in NM), not angular degrees like a VOR. The sensitivity (full scale) changes depending on whether in Enroute, Terminal, or Approach mode.

q.t: What is meant by the term "terrestrial navigation"?
o: Orientation by instrument readings during visual flight
Orientation by ground features during visual flight
Orientation by GPS during visual flight
Orientation by ground celestial object during visual flight
q.e: Terrestrial (or pilotage) navigation involves plotting a route using visible landmarks and physical ground features on the Earth's surface.

q.t: What ground features should preferrably be used for orientation during visual flight?
q.e: Large, continuous features like major rivers, highways, and railroads are easiest to spot from altitude and form excellent "catching lines" or tracking references.

q.t: What should be considered regarding a scheduled flight over water, when land cannot be reached in case of an emergency landing?
o: Transponder code 7600 has to be set during the whole flight
Contact to the nearest ATC shall consist during the whole flight
The flight plan has to contain the exact waypoints
For all passengers there must be life jackets or lifeboats present
q.e: When a balloon or aircraft flies over water where an emergency landing on land cannot be guaranteed, life jackets (and lifeboats/life rafts where appropriate) must be carried for all persons on board. This is a regulatory requirement to ensure survival capability in case of a forced water landing.

q.t: A wind shear is...
o: a slow increase of the wind speed in altitudes above 13000 ft.
a meteorological downslope wind phenomenon in the alps.
a vertical or horizontal change of wind speed and wind direction.
a wind speed change of more than 15 kt.
q.e: Wind shear is a change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance, either horizontally or vertically. It can be caused by frontal systems, thunderstorms, inversions, terrain, or jet streams. Wind shear is particularly hazardous during take-off and landing when aircraft are at low speed and altitude.

q.t: Which weather phenomenon is typically associated with wind shear?
q.e: Thunderstorms produce the most severe wind shear encountered in aviation, due to powerful updrafts, downdrafts, microbursts, and gust fronts. The outflow boundary from a thunderstorm can create sudden and dramatic wind direction/speed changes close to the ground — extremely dangerous for balloons and aircraft.

q.t: When do you expect wind shear?
o: During a summer day with calm winds
In calm wind in cold weather
q.e: Wind shear commonly occurs at inversion layers, where the wind regime changes sharply with altitude. The temperature inversion creates a stable boundary that separates different air masses with potentially very different wind speeds and directions. This is a significant hazard for balloon operations.

q.t: Wake turbulence is caused by...
o: wind shear at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
jet blast behind a turbine engine.
turbulence at the downwind side of a mountain range.
pressure compensation at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
q.e: Wake turbulence (wingtip vortices) is created by pressure equalisation at the wingtip between the high-pressure region below and the low-pressure region above the wing. The resulting spiralling vortices trail behind the aircraft, strongest behind heavy aircraft in slow, clean flight.

q.t: Wake turbulence is particularly strong...
q.e: Wake turbulence intensity is inversely related to airspeed — it is strongest when the aircraft is flying at low speed (high angle of attack) as in final approach or just after take-off. The vortices are most concentrated and energetic at these conditions because of the greater pressure differential across the wing.

q.t: During buildup of a gas balloon, sacks with sand are hooked up. The end of the hooks should be directed...
q.e: During balloon inflation, ballast bag hooks should be directed inward (inside) to prevent them from accidentally catching on net ropes or other equipment during the inflation process. Outward-facing hooks are a snagging hazard that could damage the net or cause a ballast bag to release prematurely.

q.t: Where has the ballast aboard a gas balloon to be stored during cruise?
o: at the outside wall of the basket
q.e: Ballast must be stored inside the basket during cruise to maintain it accessible for the pilot and to keep the centre of gravity stable. Externally hanging ballast could swing and affect stability, and must be accessible quickly in an emergency requiring rapid descent or climb.

q.t: Before buildup, the buildup team has to be informed about correct behaviour at sudden critical situations how?
q.e: The balloon pilot is responsible for briefing the ground crew (buildup team) on emergency procedures before inflation begins. This briefing must cover what to do in case of sudden wind, envelope tears, or other critical situations. The pilot is the authority and must ensure the team is prepared.

q.t: A balloon pilot decides to use one or more separate gas containers for initial heating during buildup. To ensure a safe buildup...
o: to expedite take-off, the gas containers have to be stored outside.
no separate gas containers are allowed during buildup.
the gas containers have to be fixed safely inside the basket.
two gas containers (one inside, one outside) are to be used.
q.e: Any gas containers used during buildup must be securely fixed inside the basket to prevent them from rolling, tipping, or being displaced during inflation. Unsecured containers are a serious safety risk — they could damage equipment, cause gas leaks, or injure personnel if they fall over.

q.t: How can expanding filling gas be released in case the filling port of a gas balloon cannot be opened during cruise?
o: By releasing the filling port cables
q.e: If the standard filling port (appendix) is blocked and the lifting gas needs to be vented to prevent over-pressure damage to the envelope, gas can be released through the emergency opening (a separate emergency vent). This is a safety feature to prevent envelope rupture due to thermal expansion.

q.t: What has to be expected during descent above a heated water surface?
q.e: A heated water surface causes thermals — rising warm air. As the balloon descends into warmer air over heated water, it encounters rising air that reduces the rate of descent (provides additional buoyancy). The warmer air also has lower density, slightly increasing buoyancy.

q.t: What has to be considered before a balloon ride across water surfaces?
o: A transponder has to be installed and carried aboard
For all people inside the basket life jackets have to be carried aboard
A flight plan with detailed routing has to be filed.
Continuous radio communication has to be established with air traffic control
q.e: Before any flight over water where a forced landing on water is possible, life jackets must be carried for all persons on board. This is a fundamental safety requirement — water landings are extremely hazardous, and personal flotation devices dramatically increase survival chances.

q.t: Environmental air temperature and filling gas temperature are the same. Now, the free balloon descends into warmer air. What statement is correct?
q.e: When the balloon descends into warmer air, the surrounding air is less dense than the cooler air above. The buoyancy (aerostatic lift) depends on the density of the surrounding air. Less dense warm air provides less buoyancy, so the net upward force decreases — but the descent force (net downward force) also decreases as the warmer air partially supports the balloon.

q.t: What has to be considered at moderate wind speeds during a balloon ride across mountainous area with cloud-free sky?
o: Lee waves and severe up- and downdrafts
