q.t: The maximum number of passengers can be found ...
q.e: The aircraft's Operating Handbook (or Flight Manual) contains all specific performance data, loading charts, and operational limitations, including maximum passenger numbers.

q.t: The Empty Mass of a gas balloon includes:
o: Ballast packages, basket, hull, valve and towing rope.
Basket, burner, ballast packages, hull, net and towing rope.
Basket, basket ring, Valve, net, hull and towing rope.
Burner, ballast packages, instruments, net and towing rope.
q.e: Empty Mass refers strictly to the permanent structural components of the balloon (basket, load ring, valve, net, envelope/hull, and towing rope). It excludes payload and consumables like ballast.

q.t: Before take-off, the balloon pilot realises that the maximum take-off mass has been exceeded by 5%. What has to be done?
o: The load has to be reduced to maximum take-off mass.
During take-off, special care has to be taken for obstacles.
With exceeding up to 5%, normal take-off can be performed.
Take-off has to be approved by the airfield manager on duty.
q.e: Maximum take-off mass is an absolute structural and aerodynamic limit. If exceeded, the pilot must offload weight until the balloon is at or below the maximum approved mass before taking off.

q.t: Information about operational limits, loading and performance about an aircraft can be taken from which document?
q.e: The Operating Handbook (Flight Manual) is the primary reference document that provides all specific performance data, weight and balance information, and operational limits for the aircraft.

q.t: What effect has air temperature on the carrying force and on maximum take-off mass of a balloon?
o: Maximum take-off mass is higher at low temperatures.
Maximum take-off mass is lower at low temperatures.
Carrying force is higher at low temperatures.
Carrying force is lower at low temperatures.
q.e: Lower air temperatures mean that the ambient air is denser. A balloon displacing denser air generates a greater aerostatic lift (carrying force).

q.t: What effect has the elevation above MSL of an airfield on the carrying force and maximum take-off mass of a balloon?
o: The higher the elevation, the lower the carrying force.
The lower the elevation, the lower the maximum take-off mass.
The lower the elevation, the higherthe maximum take-off mass.
The higher the elevation, the greater the carrying force.
q.e: Higher elevation corresponds to lower atmospheric pressure and lower air density. Because lift depends on displacing dense air, the carrying force decreases as elevation increases.

q.t: What difference will be experienced during take-off in presence of a strong surface inversion, compared to a take-off with decreasing temperature with height?
o: During climb through an inversion, less ballast must be released and/or less heating is required.
During climb through an inversion, less ballast must be released and/or more heating is required.
During climb through an inversion, more ballast must be released and/or more heating is required.
During climb through an inversion, more ballast must be released and/or less heating is required.
q.e: In an inversion, the ambient air becomes warmer (less dense) with altitude instead of colder. To maintain climb performance through this less dense air, the balloon must generate more lift by releasing more ballast or using more heat.

q.t: What has to be expected when diving into an inversion layer from above?
q.e: Descending into an inversion from above means entering a layer of much colder and denser air. This sudden increase in outside density increases the balloon's buoyancy, which slows down the rate of descent.

q.t: Given the following masses: Empty mass 240 kg, Instruments 20 kg, per gas container (full): 30 kg, per person: 80 kg. Up to which pressure altitude can the balloon climb with 5 persons and 4 gas containers in the basket, assuming temperatures 10° below ISA?
q.e: Total mass calculation: 240 (empty) + 20 (inst) + 120 (4x30 gas) + 400 (5x80 pax) = 780 kg total. By cross-referencing 780 kg on the provided performance chart at the ISA-10 temperature line, the max pressure altitude is 17000 ft.

q.t: Given the following masses: Empty mass 260 kg, Instruments 20 kg, per gas container (full): 30 kg, per person: 80 kg. Assuming temperature ISA+10, how many persons may be carried in the basket at maximum, if the balloon with 4 gas containers has to climb up to pressure altitude 12.000 ft ?
q.e: Known mass: 260 + 20 + 120 (4x30) = 400 kg. Using the chart for 12,000 ft at ISA+10, the max allowed mass is approx 640 kg. Remaining allowed mass for passengers = 640 - 400 = 240 kg. 240 kg / 80 kg per pax = 3 persons.

q.t: Given the following masses: Empty mass 260 kg, Instruments 20 kg, per gas container (full): 30 kg, per person: 80 kg. Assuming ISA temperatures, how many persons may be carried in the basket at maximum, if the balloon with 4 gas containers has to climb up to pressure altitude 9.000 ft ?
q.e: Known mass: 260 + 20 + 120 (4x30) = 400 kg. From the chart at 9,000 ft and ISA, max mass is approx 720 kg. Remaining mass for passengers = 720 - 400 = 320 kg. 320 kg / 80 kg per pax = 4 persons.

q.t: What effect has the elevation above MSL of an airfield on the carrying force and maximum take-off mass of a balloon?
o: The lower the elevation, the lower the maximum take-off mass.
The lower the elevation, the greater the carrying force.
The lower the elevation, the higherthe maximum take-off mass.
The higher the elevation, the greater the carrying force.
q.e: Lower airfield elevation means higher atmospheric pressure and therefore higher ambient air density. A balloon operating in denser air generates a greater carrying force (lift).

q.t: What is the purpose of "interception lines" in visual navigation?
o: They are used as easily recognizable guidance upon a possible loss of orientation
To visualize the range limitation from the departure aerodrome
They help to continue the flight when flight visibility drops below VFR minima
To mark the next available en-route airport during the flight
q.e: Interception lines (also known as catching features like rivers, highways, or coastlines) provide a prominent geographical backstop that a pilot can aim for to re-establish their position if lost.

q.t: The upper limit of LO R 16 equals...
q.e: According to the airspace information provided on the aeronautical chart annex (PFP-056), the upper limit for restricted area LO R 16 is established at 1500 ft MSL.

q.t: The upper limit of LO R 4 equals...
q.e: By referencing the aeronautical chart shown in annex PFP-030, the restricted area LO R 4 designates an upper vertical limit of 4500 ft MSL.

q.t: Up to which altitude is an overflight prohibited according to the NOTAM?
q.e: In NOTAM text formatting, altitude restrictions are typically specified in feet Above Mean Sea Level (AMSL), which directly translates to 9500 ft MSL.

q.t: What must be considered for cross-border flights?
q.e: International aviation regulations mandate that a flight plan must be formally submitted to air traffic services prior to conducting any flight across national borders.

q.t: During a flight, a flight plan can be filed at the...
q.e: An Airborne Flight Plan (AFIL) can be filed while in flight by contacting the regional Flight Information Service (FIS) via radio.

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a group of unlighted obstacles?
q.e: On standard ICAO charts, multiple unlighted obstacles are depicted by grouped obstacle symbols without the radiating lines that indicate lighting. This matches option 'C' in the provided annex.

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a civil airport (not international airport) with paved runway?
q.e: On ICAO visual navigation charts, a civil airport with a hard-surfaced (paved) runway is represented by a circle with an internal runway layout, corresponding to symbol 'A' in the annex.

q.t: According ICAO, what symbol indicates a general spot elevation?
q.e: A standard ICAO spot elevation is marked by a dot accompanied by a numerical elevation value in plain text, which corresponds to symbol 'C' in the provided annex.

q.t: The majority of aviation accidents are caused by...
q.e: Studies and statistics consistently show that human error (often related to decision-making, CRM, or situation awareness) is the primary contributing factor in 70-80% of aviation accidents.

q.t: The "swiss cheese model" can be used to explain the...
o: state of readiness of a pilot.
q.e: James Reason's Swiss Cheese model illustrates how an accident happens when multiple active errors and latent conditions (holes in defensive layers) align to form an error chain.

q.t: What is the percentage of oxygen in the atmosphere at 6000 ft?
q.e: The composition of the atmosphere (approx 21% oxygen, 78% nitrogen) remains constant up to about 300,000 feet. What decreases at altitude is the partial pressure of oxygen, not the percentage.

q.t: What is the percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere?
q.e: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the Earth's atmosphere, making up approximately 78% of dry air by volume.

q.t: At which altitude is the atmospheric pressure approximately half the MSL value (1013 hPa)?
q.e: Atmospheric pressure halves approximately every 18,000 feet (5,500 meters). Therefore, at FL180, the pressure is roughly 500 hPa.

q.t: Air consists of oxygen, nitrogen and other gases. What is the approximate percentage of other gases?
q.e: The atmosphere is roughly 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases (primarily argon, carbon dioxide, and trace gases).

q.t: Carbon monoxide poisoning can be caused by...
q.e: Smoking introduces significant amounts of carbon monoxide into the bloodstream, which binds to hemoglobin with high affinity and reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity.

q.t: Which of the following symptoms may indicate hypoxia?
o: Blue marks all over the body
Blue discolouration of lips and fingernails
Muscle cramps in the upper body area
Joint pain in knees and feet
q.e: Cyanosis, which is a bluish discoloration of the lips and fingernails, is a classic visible symptom of hypoxia due to deoxygenated blood.

q.t: Which of the human senses is most influenced by hypoxia?
q.e: The eyes, specifically the rods used for night vision, are highly sensitive to oxygen deprivation. Vision degradation is often the first physiological sign of hypoxia.

q.t: From which altitude on does the body usually react to the decreasing atmospheric pressure?
q.e: While significant symptoms usually occur higher, the body's physiological reactions (like impaired night vision and subtle cognitive changes) begin at approximately 7,000 feet due to lowering oxygen partial pressure.

q.t: Which altitude marks the lower limit where the the body is unable to completely compensate the effects of the low atmospheric pressure?
q.e: Around 10,000 to 12,000 feet, the body's compensatory mechanisms (increased breathing/heart rate) become insufficient to maintain optimal blood oxygen saturation, leading to hypoxia.

q.t: What is the function of the red blood cells (erythrocytes)?
q.e: Erythrocytes (red blood cells) contain hemoglobin, a protein responsible for picking up oxygen in the lungs and transporting it to tissues throughout the body.

q.t: Which characteristic is important when choosing sunglasses used by pilots?
q.e: Pilots must use non-polarised sunglasses because polarised lenses can mask the glare from other aircraft and make LCD displays in the cockpit unreadable.

q.t: In which situation is it NOT possible to achieve a pressure compensation between the middle ear and the environment?
o: During a light and slow climb
Breathing takes place using the mouth only
q.e: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat. If it is blocked (e.g., by a cold or inflammation), pressure cannot equalize, leading to severe ear pain and potential eardrum rupture during descents.

q.t: Visual illusions are mostly caused by...
q.e: Visual illusions occur when the brain incorrectly interprets visual cues from the environment, often due to a lack of standard references (e.g., featureless terrain, sloping clouds).

q.t: The average decrease of blood alcohol level for an adult in one hour is approximately...
q.e: On average, the human body metabolizes alcohol at a rate of roughly 0.01% BAC (Blood Alcohol Concentration) per hour.

q.t: A risk factor for decompression sickness is...
q.e: Scuba diving dissolves nitrogen under pressure into body tissues. If a pilot flies too soon after diving, the reduced cabin pressure can cause the nitrogen to form bubbles, leading to decompression sickness (the bends).

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the short-term memory?
o: It can store 5 (±2) items for 1 to 2 minutes
It can store 3 (±1) items for 5 to 10 seconds
It can store 7 (±2) items for 10 to 20 seconds
It can store 10 (±5) items for 30 to 60 seconds
q.e: Short-term (working) memory has a very limited capacity, typically holding about 7 ± 2 items for roughly 10 to 20 seconds without active rehearsal.

q.t: For what approximate time period can the short-time memory store information?
q.e: Information in short-term memory decays rapidly, usually within 10 to 20 seconds, unless it is mentally repeated or written down.

q.t: What is a latent error?
o: An error which has an immediate effect on the controls
An error which is made by the pilot actively and consciously
An error which remains undetected in the system for a long time
An error which only has consequences after landing
q.e: A latent error is a dormant flaw in a system (e.g., poor design, bad management decisions, lack of training) that remains undetected until triggered by an active failure.

q.t: The ongoing process to monitor the current flight situation is called...
q.e: Situational Awareness is the perception of environmental elements, comprehension of their meaning, and projection of their status in the near future.

q.t: Regarding the communication model, how can the use of the same code during radio communication be ensured?
o: By the use of proper headsets
By the use of radio phraseology
By using radios certified for aviation use only
q.e: Standardized radio phraseology ensures that the sender and receiver use exactly the same "code," minimizing misunderstandings and improving flight safety.

q.t: In what different ways can a risk be handled appropriately?
q.e: Standard risk management strategies involve Avoiding the risk, Reducing its impact/probability, Transferring it (e.g., insurance), or consciously Accepting it if it is within safe margins.

q.t: Under which circumstances is it more likely to accept higher risks?
o: During check flights due to a high level of nervousness
During flight planning when excellent weather is forecast
If there is not enough information available
q.e: Group dynamics (like "groupthink" or peer pressure) can dilute an individual's sense of responsibility, making them more likely to accept risks they would normally reject alone.

q.t: Which dangerous attitudes are often combined?
q.e: The "Macho" attitude (proving oneself) often pairs with "Invulnerability" (it won't happen to me), creating a highly hazardous mindset where extreme risks are ignored.

q.t: What is an indication for a macho attitude?
o: Quick resignation in complex and critical situations
Comprehensive risk assessment when faced with unfamiliar situations
Risky flight maneuvers to impress spectators on ground
q.e: Taking unnecessary risks or performing dangerous maneuvers to show off or impress others is the defining characteristic of the "Macho" hazardous attitude.

q.t: Which factor can lead to human error?
o: To be doubtful if something looks unclear or ambiguous
The bias to see what we expect to see
q.e: Confirmation bias—the tendency to perceive what we expect to perceive rather than reality (e.g., misreading an altimeter because you expect a certain altitude)—is a major cause of error.

q.t: What is the best combination of traits with respect to the individual attitude and behaviour for a pilot?
q.e: Aviation psychology suggests an ideal pilot profile is somewhat extroverted (good communication, teamwork, CRM) and highly emotionally stable (handles stress well, doesn't panic).

q.t: The ideal level of arousal is at which point in the diagram? (HPL- 002)
q.e: On the Yerkes-Dodson curve, the peak of the curve (designated as Point B in this specific chart) represents optimal arousal where performance is highest. Too little causes boredom; too much causes panic.

q.t: At which point in the diagram will a pilot find himself to be overstrained? (HPL-002)
q.e: Point D represents the far right of the Yerkes-Dodson curve, indicating a state of being overstrained (high stress/arousal), where performance drops sharply due to cognitive overload.

q.t: Which of the following qualities are influenced by stress? 1. Attention 2. Concentration 3. Responsiveness 4. Memory
q.e: High stress negatively impacts nearly all cognitive functions, including attention (tunnel vision), concentration, reaction time (responsiveness), and working memory.

q.t: What clouds and weather may result from an humid and instable air mass, that is pushed against a chain of mountains by the predominant wind and forced to rise?
o: Embedded CB with thunderstorms and showers of hail and/or rain.
Overcast low stratus (high fog) with no precipitation.
Smooth, unstructured NS cloud with light drizzle or snow (during winter).
Thin Altostratus and Cirrostratus clouds with light and steady precipitation.
q.e: When unstable, humid air is forced to rise over mountains (orographic lifting), it triggers deep convective development. In unstable conditions, cumulus clouds grow rapidly into cumulonimbus (CB) with associated thunderstorms, hail, and heavy showers.

q.t: What type of fog emerges if humid and almost saturated air, is forced to rise upslope of hills or shallow mountains by the prevailling wind?
q.e: Orographic fog (hill fog) forms when moist air is forced to rise along hillsides or shallow mountains. As it rises, it cools to its dew point and condensation occurs.

q.t: What is the gas composition of "air"?
o: Oxygen 21 % Water vapour 78 % Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1 %
Nitrogen 21 % Oxygen 78 % Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1 %
Oxygen 21 % Nitrogen 78 % Noble gases / carbon dioxide 1 %
q.e: Dry air is composed of approximately 78% nitrogen (N2), 21% oxygen (O2), and about 1% other gases (mainly argon, plus CO2 and trace gases).

q.t: Weather phenomena are most common to be found in which atmospheric layer?
q.e: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, containing about 75% of the atmosphere's mass and virtually all water vapour. Nearly all weather phenomena occur here.

q.t: What is the mass of a "cube of air" with the edges 1 m long, at MSL according ISA?
q.e: According to the ICAO Standard Atmosphere (ISA), standard air density at Mean Sea Level is 1.225 kg/m³. Therefore a cubic metre of air weighs exactly 1.225 kg.

q.t: At what rate does the temperature change with increasing height according to ISA (ICAO Standard Atmosphere) within the troposphere?
q.e: The ISA standard temperature lapse rate in the troposphere is a steady decrease of approximately 2°C per 1000 ft (or exactly 6.5°C per 1000 m).

q.t: What is the mean height of the tropopause according to ISA (ICAO Standard Atmosphere)?
q.e: The tropopause in the ICAO Standard Atmosphere is defined at a standard altitude of 11,000 meters (approximately 36,089 ft).

q.t: The term "tropopause" is defined as...
o: the layer above the troposphere showing an increasing temperature.
the height above which the temperature starts to decrease.
the boundary area between the mesosphere and the stratosphere.
the boundary area between the troposphere and the stratosphere.
q.e: The tropopause is the transition boundary zone between the weather-active troposphere below and the stable stratosphere above.

q.t: Temperatures will be given by meteorological aviation services in Europe in which unit?
q.e: European aviation meteorological services (METARs, TAFs) report temperatures in degrees Celsius (°C) in accordance with ICAO and EASA regional standards.

q.t: What is meant by "inversion layer"?
o: An atmospheric layer where temperature increases with increasing height
A boundary area between two other layers within the atmosphere
An atmospheric layer with constant temperature with increasing height
An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases with increasing height
q.e: An inversion layer is an anomaly where temperature increases with altitude, "inverting" the normal lapse rate. This highly stable air traps moisture and prevents convection.

q.t: What is meant by "isothermal layer"?
o: A boundary area between two other layers within the atmosphere
An atmospheric layer where temperature decreases with increasing height
An atmospheric layer where temperature increases with increasing height
An atmospheric layer with constant temperature with increasing height
q.e: An isothermal layer maintains a constant temperature as altitude increases. The lower stratosphere is a classic example of an isothermal layer.

q.t: The temperature lapse rate with increasing height within the troposphere according ISA is...
q.e: The formal ISA standard environmental lapse rate is exactly 0.65°C per 100 meters (which translates to roughly 2°C per 1,000 feet).

q.t: Which process may result in an inversion layer at about 5000 ft (1500 m) height?
o: Intensive sunlight insolation during a warm summer day
Ground cooling by radiation during the night
Advection of cool air in the upper troposphere
Widespread descending air within a high pressure area
q.e: Subsidence inversions form when a broad layer of air sinks (subsides) in a high-pressure system, compressing and warming as it descends, often settling around 5,000 ft.

q.t: An inversion layer close to the ground can be caused by...
o: thickening of clouds in medium layers.
q.e: Radiation inversions form near the ground at night when the surface cools rapidly by emitting infrared radiation, cooling the air immediately above it.

q.t: What is the ISA standard pressure at FL 180 (5500 m)?
q.e: At FL180 (approximately 18,000 ft or 5,500 m), atmospheric pressure is approximately halved compared to MSL, making it roughly 500 hPa.

q.t: Which processes result in decreasing air density?
q.e: Air density decreases when it expands due to heat (increasing temperature) or when the ambient pressure pushing the molecules together drops (decreasing pressure).

q.t: The pressure at MSL in ISA conditions is...
q.e: The ICAO Standard Atmosphere precisely defines Mean Sea Level (MSL) pressure as 1013.25 hPa (equivalent to 29.92 inHg).

q.t: The barometric altimeter indicates height above...
q.e: A barometric altimeter mechanically measures the vertical distance between the ambient pressure and the specific reference pressure dialed into its subscale window.

q.t: The altimeter can be checked on the ground by setting...
o: QNE and checking that the indication shows zero on the ground.
QFF and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QNH and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
QFE and comparing the indication with the airfield elevation.
q.e: By setting the local QNH on the ground, the altimeter should accurately read the official elevation of the airfield.

q.t: The barometric altimeter with QNH setting indicates...
o: height above the pressure level at airfield elevation.
q.e: QNH is the pressure setting that provides indicated altitude (height above Mean Sea Level).

q.t: How can wind speed and wind direction be derived from surface weather charts?
o: By annotations from the text part of the chart
By alignment of lines of warm- and cold fronts.
By alignment and distance of isobaric lines
By alignment and distance of hypsometric lines
q.e: Isobars show wind direction (flowing roughly parallel to the lines) and wind speed (closer lines mean a stronger pressure gradient and faster winds).

q.t: Which force causes "wind"?
q.e: The fundamental driver of all wind is the Pressure Gradient Force — air accelerating from an area of high pressure toward an area of low pressure.

q.t: Above the friction layer, with a prevailing pressure gradient, the wind direction is...
o: at an angle of 30° to the isobars towards low pressure.
q.e: Above the friction layer, the Coriolis force turns the wind until it balances the pressure gradient force, resulting in geostrophic wind that blows parallel to the isobars.

q.t: Which of the stated surfaces will reduce the wind speed most due to ground friction?
o: Flat land, lots of vegetation cover
Flat land, deserted land, no vegetation
q.e: Friction is determined by surface roughness. Mountainous terrain covered in vegetation presents the highest physical resistance, reducing wind speed the most.

q.t: The movement of air flowing together is called...
q.e: Convergence is the meteorological term for air masses flowing together horizontally, which subsequently forces the air to rise.

q.t: The movement of air flowing apart is called...
q.e: Divergence describes air spreading out horizontally away from a central region, typically associated with high-pressure systems and descending air.

q.t: What weather development will result from convergence at ground level?
q.e: When air converges at the surface, it has nowhere to go but up. This ascending air cools, moisture condenses, and clouds form.

q.t: When air masses meet each other head on, how is this referred to and what air movements will follow?
o: Divergence resulting in air being lifted
Convergence resulting in air being lifted
q.e: Meeting head-on is convergence. Because the air cannot go into the ground, it is forced upward (lifted), creating clouds and precipitation.

q.t: What are the air masses that Central Europe is mainly influenced by?
o: Polar cold air and tropical warm air
q.e: Central Europe sits in the mid-latitudes, acting as the primary boundary zone between cold Polar air from the north and warm Tropical air from the south.

q.t: With regard to global circulation within the atmosphere, where does polar cold air meets subtropical warm air?
o: At the subtropical high pressure belt
q.e: The polar front is the continuous, dynamic boundary in the mid-latitudes where cold polar air clashes with warmer subtropical air.

q.t: Foehn conditions usually develop with...
o: instability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
stability, widespread air blown against a mountain ridge.
stability, high pressure area with calm wind.
instability, high pressure area with calm wind.
q.e: Foehn winds develop when a stable, widespread air mass is forced over a mountain ridge, warming dynamically as it descends the lee side.

q.t: What type of turbulence is typically found close to the ground on the lee side during Foehn conditions?
q.e: Rotor turbulence forms at the surface underneath mountain waves on the lee side of a range during Foehn conditions. It is highly turbulent and dangerous.

q.t: Light turbulence always has to be expected...
o: above cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
below cumulus clouds due to thermal convection.
below stratiform clouds in medium layers.
q.e: Thermals (rising columns of warm air) generate cumulus clouds. Flying below these clouds means flying through the active convective currents feeding them.

q.t: Moderate to severe turbulence has to be expected...
o: on the lee side of a mountain range when rotor clouds are present.
below thick cloud layers on the windward side of a mountain range.
with the appearance of extended low stratus clouds (high fog).
q.e: Rotor clouds mark areas of severe mechanical turbulence and violent updrafts/downdrafts caused by mountain waves on the lee side of a range.

q.t: Which answer contains every state of water found in the atmosphere?
q.e: Water exists simultaneously in the atmosphere as a gas (water vapour), a liquid (cloud droplets, rain), and a solid (ice crystals, snow).

q.t: How do dew point and relative humidity change with decreasing temperature?
o: Dew point increases, relative humidity decreases
Dew point remains constant, relative humidity decreases
Dew point remains constant, relative humidity increases
Dew point decreases, relative humidity increases
q.e: If temperature drops but absolute moisture content remains the same, the dew point is constant, but the air approaches saturation, so relative humidity increases.

q.t: How do spread and relative humidity change with increasing temperature?
o: Spread remains constant, relative humidity increases
Spread remains constant, relative humidity decreases
q.e: As temperature increases, the capacity of the air to hold water grows. The spread (gap between temp and dew point) widens, and relative humidity decreases.

q.t: The "spread" is defined as...
o: difference between dew point and condensation point.
relation of actual to maximum possible humidity of air.
difference between actual temperature and dew point.
maximum amount of water vapour that can be contained in air.
q.e: The temperature-dew point spread is the physical difference (in degrees) between the current air temperature and the dew point.

q.t: With other factors remaining constant, decreasing temperature results in...
o: decreasing spread and decreasing relative humidity.
decreasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
increasing spread and decreasing relative humidity.
increasing spread and increasing relative humidity.
q.e: Cooling the air brings the temperature closer to the dew point (decreasing the spread). As the spread shrinks, the air approaches saturation (increasing relative humidity).

q.t: What process causes latent heat being released into the upper troposphere?
q.e: Latent heat is absorbed during evaporation and released during condensation. When clouds form, this phase change releases heat into the surrounding air.

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate is...
o: proportional to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
higher than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
lower than the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
equal to the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
q.e: Because condensing water releases latent heat, a rising parcel of saturated air cools slower (approx. 1.5°C/1000 ft) than dry air (3°C/1000 ft).

q.t: The dry adiabatic lapse rate has a value of...
q.e: The Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR) is fixed by physical laws at 1.0°C per 100 meters (or approximately 3°C per 1,000 feet).

q.t: The saturated adiabatic lapse rate should be assumed with a mean value of:
q.e: While it varies with temperature and pressure, standard meteorological calculations use a mean Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR) of 0.6°C per 100 meters.

q.t: What weather conditions may be expected during conditionally unstable conditions?
o: Towering cumulus, isolated showers of rain or thunderstorms
Layered clouds up to high levels, prolonged rain or snow
Shallow cumulus clouds with base at medium levels
Sky clear of clouds, sunshine, low winds
q.e: Conditional instability means air is stable if dry, but unstable if saturated. If lifted to saturation, it erupts into deep convection (towering cumulus, Cb).

q.t: Which conditions are likely for the formation of advection fog?
o: Cold, humid air moves over a warm ocean
Humidity evaporates from warm, humid ground into cold air
Warm, humid air cools during a cloudy night
Warm, humid air moves over a cold surface
q.e: Advection fog forms when moist, relatively warm air is blown horizontally (advected) over a cooler surface, chilling the air from below until it saturates.

q.t: Clouds are basically distinguished by what types?
q.e: Meteorologically, all clouds fall into two main families based on air stability: Cumuliform (heaped/convective) and Stratiform (layered/stable).

q.t: Clouds in high layers are referred to as...
q.e: The prefix "Cirro-" (meaning "curl of hair") denotes high-altitude ice clouds (e.g., Cirrus, Cirrostratus).

q.t: What weather phenomenon designated by "2" has to be expected on the lee side during "Foehn" conditions?
q.e: Altocumulus lenticularis (lens-shaped clouds) form in the crests of mountain standing waves and indicate severe mountain wave turbulence.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show? (MET-002)
q.e: The image shows Cumulus clouds — detached, fluffy, cauliflower-like heaps with flat bases, indicating fair-weather thermal convection.

q.t: What cloud type does the picture show? (MET-004)
q.e: The image shows Cirrus clouds — delicate, wispy, fibrous hair-like strands made entirely of ice crystals at very high altitudes.

q.t: What factor may affect the top of cumulus clouds?
o: The presence of an inversion layer
q.e: An inversion layer acts like a physical lid. The warm air in the inversion stops the rising convective currents, preventing cumulus clouds from growing taller.

q.t: What factors may indicate a tendency to fog formation?
q.e: A low temperature-dew point spread means the air is nearly saturated. If the temperature continues to decrease, saturation is reached, and fog will form.

q.t: What condition may prevent the formation of "radiation fog"?
q.e: Overcast clouds act like a thermal blanket, absorbing and radiating heat back to the ground. This prevents the surface from cooling enough to form radiation fog.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "advection fog"?
o: Warm, moist air is moved across cold ground areas
Cold, moist air is being moved across warm ground areas
Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
q.e: Advection fog requires wind to push a warm, humid air mass horizontally over a cold surface, chilling the air to its dew point.

q.t: What process results in the formation of "orographic fog" ("hill fog")?
o: Prolonged radiation during nights clear of clouds
Warm, moist air is moved across a hill or a mountain range
Evaporation from warm, moist ground area into very cold air
Cold, moist air mixes with warm, moist air
q.e: As wind blows moist air against a mountain, the air is forced upward, expanding and cooling adiabatically until it condenses into "hill fog".

q.t: What factors are required for the formation of precipitation in clouds?
o: The presence of an inversion layer
Calm winds and intensive sunlight insolation
q.e: Updrafts keep tiny water droplets suspended in the cloud until they collide and merge (coalesce) into drops heavy enough to fall as precipitation.

q.t: The formation of medium to large precipitation particles requires...
q.e: Strong updrafts hold droplets aloft much longer, allowing them to collect more water or ice before eventually overcoming gravity and falling.

q.t: Which type of cloud is associated with prolonged rain?
q.e: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark, widespread cloud layer that delivers continuous, prolonged precipitation.

q.t: Regarding the type of cloud, precipitation is classified as...
q.e: Precipitation is classified by its cloud source: Stratiform clouds produce steady "rain", while cumuliform clouds produce intermittent "showers of rain".

q.t: How is an air mass described when moving to Central Europe via the Russian continent during winter?
q.e: Air originating over the vast, cold landmass of Russia in winter is dry (Continental) and cold (Polar).

q.t: The character of an air mass is given by what properties?
o: Temperatures at origin and present region
Region of origin and track during movement
q.e: An air mass inherits its baseline properties from its source region, and is subsequently modified by the surface it tracks over as it moves.

q.t: The symbol labeled (1) as shown in the picture is a / an... (Solid line with triangles)
q.e: A solid line with triangles pointing in the direction of movement is the international meteorological symbol for a cold front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (2) as shown in the picture is a / an... (Solid line with semi-circles)
q.e: A solid line with semi-circles pointing in the direction of movement is the standard symbol for a warm front.

q.t: The symbol labeled (3) as shown in the picture is a / an... (Line with alternating triangles and semi-circles)
q.e: A line with alternating triangles and semi-circles represents an occluded front, where a cold front has caught up to a warm front.

q.t: What cloud sequence can typically be observed during the passage of a warm front?
o: Squall line with showers of rain and thunderstorms (Cb), gusting wind followed by cumulus clouds with isolated showers of rain
Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds and warming during summer; formation of extended high fog layers during winter
Cirrus, thickening altostratus and altocumulus clouds, lowering cloud base with rain, nimbostratus
In coastal areas during daytime wind from the coast and forming of cumulus clouds, dissipation of clouds during evening and night
q.e: A warm front approaches gradually: high Cirrus first, thickening into Altostratus, and finally lowering into Nimbostratus with steady rain.

q.t: What clouds and weather can typically be observed during the passage of a cold front?
o: Strongly developed cumulus clouds (Cb) with showers of rain and thunderstorms, gusting wind followed by cumulus clouds with isolated showers of rain
Wind becoming calm, dissipation of clouds and warming during summer; formation of extended high fog layers during winter
Cirrus, thickening altostratus and altocumulus clouds, lowering cloud base with rain, nimbostratus
In coastal areas during daytime wind from the coast and forming of cumulus clouds, dissipation of clouds during evening and night
q.e: Cold fronts violently force warm air upward, causing massive instability, generating Cumulonimbus (Cb), thunderstorms, heavy showers, and gusty winds.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected within the warm sector of a polar front low during summer time?
o: Visibilty less than 1000 m, cloud-covered ground
Moderate to good visibility, scattered clouds
Moderate visibility, heavy showers and thunderstorms
Good visibility, some isolated high clouds
q.e: The warm sector (between the warm front and trailing cold front) generally features warm air, scattered fair-weather cumulus, and moderate to good visibility.

q.t: What visual flight conditions can be expected after the passage of a cold front?
o: Poor visibility, formation of overcast or ground-covering stratus clouds, snow
Medium visibility with lowering cloud bases, onset of prolonged precipitation
Good visiblity, formation of cumulus clouds with showers of rain or snow
Scattered cloud layers, visbility more than 5 km, formation of shallow cumulus clouds
q.e: Behind a cold front, the air is cold and unstable. It triggers scattered cumulus and isolated showers, but visibility between showers is typically excellent.

q.t: A boundary between a cold polar air mass and a warm subtropical air mass showing no horizontal displacement is called...
q.e: When two contrasting air masses meet but neither is advancing against the other, the boundary stalls and is termed a stationary front.

q.t: What is the usual direction of movement of a polar front low?
o: To the northeast during winter, to the southeast during summer
Parallel to the the warm-sector isobars
To the northwest during winter, to the southwest during summer
Parallel to the warm front line to the south
q.e: Low pressure systems are generally steered by upper-level winds, which align closely parallel to the surface isobars found within the system's warm sector.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed during the passage of a polar front low?
o: Falling pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, falling pressure behind the cold front
Falling pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, rising pressure behind the cold front
Rising pressure in front of the warm front, constant pressure within the warm sector, rising pressure behind the cold front
Rising pressure in front of the warm front, rising pressure within the warm sector, falling pressure behind the cold front
q.e: Pressure falls as the low approaches, flattens out in the warm sector, and rises sharply once the heavy, dense air of the cold front passes.

q.t: What pressure pattern can be observed when a cold front is passing?
q.e: Pressure drops to its lowest point right at the frontal boundary. Immediately after the cold front passes, the dense cold air causes pressure to surge upward.

q.t: What change of wind direction can be expected during the passage of a polar front low in Central Europe?
o: Backing wind during passage of the warm front, veering wind during passage of the cold front
Backing wind during passage of the warm front, backing wind during passage of the cold front
Veering wind during passage of the warm front, backing wind during passage of the cold front
Veering wind during passage of the warm front, veering wind during passage of the cold front
q.e: In the Northern Hemisphere, passing frontal boundaries typically cause the wind to veer (shift clockwise, e.g., from South to Southwest to Northwest).

q.t: What cloud type can typically be observed across widespread high pressure areas during summer?
q.e: High pressure means subsiding (sinking) air, which suppresses deep cloud development, resulting in clear skies or isolated, shallow Cumulus clouds.

q.t: What pressure pattern may result from cold-air inflow in high tropospheric layers?
o: Formation of a low in the upper troposphere
Formation of a large ground low
Formation of a high in the upper troposphere
q.e: Cold air is denser and heavier. When it flows into the upper troposphere, it lowers the heights of pressure levels aloft, creating an upper-level low (or trough).

q.t: Cold air inflow in high tropospheric layers may result in...
q.e: Cold air aloft above warm surface air creates a very steep environmental lapse rate. This instability fuels deep convection, showers, and thunderstorms.

q.t: What weather phenomena have to be expected around an upper-level trough?
o: Formation of high stratus clouds, ground-covering cloud bases
Calm weather, formation of lifted fog layers
Calm wind, forming of shallow cumulus clouds
q.e: An upper-level trough brings cold air aloft, forcing upward vertical motion that leads to instability, showers, and thunderstorms.

q.t: What frontal line divides subtropical air from polar cold air, in particular across Central Europe?
q.e: The Polar Front is the semi-permanent, global-scale boundary separating cold polar air masses from warm subtropical air masses.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Changing weather with passing of frontal lines
Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
q.e: Summer high pressure systems feature subsiding air that warms and dries as it sinks. This prevents storm formation, leading to calm, sunny weather.

q.t: What weather conditions in Central Europe are typically found in high pressure areas during summer?
o: Small isobar spacing with strong prevailing northerly winds
Large isobar spacing with calm winds, formation of local wind systems
Large isobar spacing with strong prevailing westerly winds
Small isobar spacing with calm winds, formation of local wind systems
q.e: High pressure means a weak pressure gradient, shown by widely spaced (large) isobars. The resulting calm winds allow local thermal breezes to dominate.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected in high pressure areas during winter?
o: Changing weather with passing of frontal lines
Calm winds and widespread areas with high fog
Calm weather and cloud dissipation, few high Cu
q.e: Winter highs cause strong surface temperature inversions. Moisture is trapped in the cold, stagnant air near the ground, resulting in widespread, persistent high fog.

q.t: What wind conditions can be expected in areas showing large distances between isobars?
o: Formation of local wind systems with strong prevailing westerly winds
Strong prevailing westerly winds with rapid veering
Variable winds, formation of local wind systems
Strong prevailing easterly winds with rapid backing
q.e: Large distances between isobars indicate a weak pressure gradient force. This results in calm or variable winds, allowing local thermal effects to take over.

q.t: What weather conditions can be expected during "Foehn" on the windward side of a mountain range?
o: Layered clouds, mountains obscured, poor visibility, moderate or heavy rain
Scattered cumulus clouds with showers and thunderstorms
Calm wind and forming of high stratus clouds (high fog)
Dissipating clouds with unusual warming, accompanied by strong, gusty winds
q.e: On the windward (stau) side, moist air is forced up the mountain, causing massive condensation, overcast layered clouds, heavy rain/snow, and obscured peaks.

q.t: What situation may result in the occurrence of severe wind shear?
o: When a shower is visible close to the airfield
Cross-country flying below Cu clouds with about 4 octas coverage
During final approach, 30 min after a heavy shower has passed the airfield
Flying ahead of a warm front with visible Ci clouds
q.e: Showers and thunderstorms produce violent, cold downdrafts that hit the ground and spread outward rapidly as gust fronts, generating severe wind shear.

q.t: What conditions are favourable for the formation of thunderstorms?
o: Warm and dry air, strong inversion layer
Clear night over land, cold air and patches of fog
Calm winds and cold air, overcast cloud cover with St or As.
Warm humid air, conditionally unstable environmental lapse rate
q.e: Thunderstorms require three key ingredients: high moisture (humid air), instability (conditionally unstable lapse rate), and a lifting mechanism.

q.t: What conditions are mandatory for the formation of thermal thunderstorms?
o: Absolutely stable atmosphere, high temperature and high humidity
Absolutely stable atmosphere, high temperature and low humidity
Conditionally unstable atmosphere, high temperature and high humidity
Conditionally unstable atmosphere, low temperature and low humidity
q.e: Thermal thunderstorms form due to intense surface heating. They require high humidity for energy and a conditionally unstable atmosphere to allow the heated air to rise.

q.t: With regard to thunderstorms, strong up- and downdrafts appear during the...
q.e: The mature stage is the most violent part of a thunderstorm's lifecycle, characterized by the simultaneous presence of massive updrafts and heavy precipitation-driven downdrafts.

q.t: Which stage of a thunderstorm is dominated by updrafts?
q.e: The initial or "Cumulus" stage consists entirely of continuous updrafts that build the cloud vertically. No precipitation falls during this stage.

q.t: Heavy downdrafts and strong wind shear close to the ground can be expected...
o: during approach to an airfield at the coast with a strong sea breeze.
during cold, clear nights with the formation of radiation fog.
during warm summer days with high, flatted Cu clouds.
near the rainfall areas of heavy showers or thunderstorms.
q.e: The massive weight of precipitation falling from a Cumulonimbus pulls cold air down with it, creating a violent downdraft that hits the ground and causes extreme wind shear.

q.t: What phenomenon is caused by cold air downdrafts with precipitation from a fully developed thunderstorm cloud?
q.e: When a cold downdraft hits the ground and spreads horizontally, its leading edge acts like a mini cold front known as a gust front, characterized by violent winds.

q.t: What kind of reduction in visibility is not very sensitive to changes in temperature?
q.e: Haze consists of dry microscopic particles (dust, smoke, pollutants) rather than water droplets, so it does not evaporate when temperatures rise like fog or mist does.

q.t: Information about pressure patterns and frontal situation can be found in which chart?
q.e: Surface weather charts (Synoptic charts) are specifically designed to map out isobars, Highs, Lows, and frontal boundaries at ground level.

q.t: Which weather chart shows the actual air pressure as in MSL along with pressure centers and fronts?
q.e: The standard surface weather chart maps atmospheric pressure reduced to Mean Sea Level (MSL) using isobars, along with the positions of pressure centers and fronts.

q.t: What information can be obtained from satallite images?
o: Flight visibility, ground visibility, and ground contact
Overview of cloud covers and front lines
Temperature and dew point of environmental air
q.e: Satellites capture images from space, providing an excellent visual overview of cloud coverage, storm systems, and the alignment of major weather fronts.

q.t: What chart shows areas of precipitation?
q.e: Weather radar works by bouncing microwave pulses off water droplets and ice crystals. It is the primary tool for locating and measuring precipitation intensity.

q.t: Measured pressure distribution in MSL and corresponding frontal systems are displayed by the...
q.e: Surface weather charts summarize current or forecast weather at the surface, explicitly showing MSL isobars, highs, lows, and frontal lines.

q.t: In a METAR, "heavy rain" is designated by the identifier...
q.e: In METAR coding, the "+" prefix indicates "heavy", and "RA" is the abbreviation for Rain. Thus, +RA means heavy continuous rain.

q.t: In a METAR, "(moderate) showers of rain" are designated by the identifier...
q.e: SH signifies Showers, and "RA" signifies Rain. The absence of a "+" or "-" prefix means it is of moderate intensity.

q.t: An inversion is a layer ...
o: with increasing pressure with increasing height.
with increasing temperature with increasing height.
with constant temperature with increasing height.
with decreasing temperature with increasing height.
q.e: Normally, temperature decreases with height. An inversion is an "inverted" state where a layer of warm air sits above colder air, meaning temperature increases with height.

q.t: What can be expected for the prevailling wind with isobars on a surface weather chart showing large distances?
o: Low pressure gradients resulting in low prevailling wind
Strong pressure gradients resulting in strong prevailling wind
Strong pressure gradients resulting in low prevailling wind
Low pressure gradients resulting in strong prevailling wind
q.e: The distance between isobars indicates pressure gradient. Large distances mean a weak (low) gradient, which results in weak or calm winds.

q.t: What is referred to as mountain wind?
o: Wind blowing uphill from the valley during daytime.
Wind blowing uphill from the valley during the night.
Wind blowing down the mountain side during daytime.
Wind blowing down the mountain side during the night
q.e: At night, mountain slopes cool rapidly. The cold, dense air flows downhill into the valleys under gravity. This nocturnal down-slope flow is the "mountain wind".

q.t: Under which conditions "back side weather" ("Rückseitenwetter") can be expected?
o: During Foehn at the lee side
After passing of a warm front
After passing of a cold front
q.e: Rückseitenwetter (backside weather) describes the cold, unstable, showery, but highly visible air mass that rushes in immediately following the passage of a cold front.

q.t: What wind is reportet as 225/15 ?
q.e: Wind is reported as direction (origin) / speed. 225 degrees is Southwest. Aviation wind speed is normally reported in knots (kt).

q.t: How does air temperatur change in ISA from MSL to approx. 10.000 m height?
q.e: In the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), MSL temperature is +15°C. Cooling at 6.5°C per 1000m, the temperature at 10,000m is -50°C.

q.t: What weather is likely to be experienced during "Foehn" in the Bavarian area close to the alps?
o: High pressure area overhead Biskaya and low pressure area in Eastern Europe
Nimbostratus cloud in the southern alps, rotor clouds at the lee side, warm and dry wind
Cold, humid downhill wind on the lee side of the alps, flat pressure pattern
Nimbostratus cloud in the northern alps, rotor clouds at the windward side, warm and dry wind
q.e: In a Southern Foehn, the Italian/Austrian side gets heavy rain (Nimbostratus). Bavaria (the lee side) experiences warm, dry, gusty winds falling from the mountains, often with dangerous rotor clouds.

q.t: Mountain side updrafts can be intensified by ...
o: Solar irradiation on the lee side
thermal radiation of the windward side during the night
Solar irradiation on the windward side
By warming of upper atmospheric layers
q.e: When the sun heats the windward side of a mountain, the surface air warms and rises thermally (anabatic wind). This thermal updraft intensifies the mechanical updraft caused by the wind hitting the mountain.

q.t: The rotational axis of the Earth runs through the...
o: geographic North Pole and on the geographic South Pole.
magnetic north pole and on the magnetic south pole.
geographic North Pole and on the magnetic south pole.
magnetic north pole and on the geographic South Pole.
q.e: The Earth rotates around its geographic axis, intersecting the surface exactly at the geographic North and South Poles.

q.t: Which statement is correct with regard to the polar axis of the Earth?
o: The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is at an angle of 23.5° to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the geographic South Pole and the geographic North Pole and is perpendicular to the plane of the equator
The polar axis of the Earth crosses the magnetic south pole and the magnetic north pole and is at an angle of 66.5° to the plane of the equator
q.e: The geographic polar axis is by definition perpendicular (90 degrees) to the equatorial plane and connects the true geographic poles.

q.t: Which approximate, geometrical form describes the shape of the Earth best for navigation systems?
q.e: The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator, making an oblate ellipsoid (like WGS84) the most accurate mathematical model for modern navigation systems.

q.t: The shortest distance between two points on Earth is represented by a part of...
q.e: A great circle represents the intersection of the Earth's surface with a plane passing through the Earth's center, forming the shortest possible path between any two points.

q.t: The circumference of the Earth at the equator is approximately...
q.e: One minute of longitude at the equator equals roughly 1 NM. Since there are 360 degrees, 360 * 60 minutes = 21,600 NM.

q.t: What is the difference in latitude between A (12°53'30''N) and B (07°34'30''S)?
q.e: Since the points are in opposite hemispheres, their latitudes are added: 12°53'30" + 07°34'30" = 19°87'60", which mathematically simplifies to exactly 20°28'00".

q.t: Where are the two polar circles?
o: 23.5° north and south of the poles
23.5° north and south of the equator
q.e: The polar circles (Arctic and Antarctic) are located at roughly 66.5° N and S latitude, which is exactly 23.5° away from the 90° poles.

q.t: What is the distance between the parallels of latitude 48°N and 49°N along a meridian line?
q.e: Along a meridian, 1 minute of latitude always equals exactly 1 Nautical Mile. Therefore, 1 degree (which is 60 minutes) equals 60 NM.

q.t: What distance corresponds to one degree difference in latitude along any degree of longitude?
q.e: By definition, one minute of latitude is 1 Nautical Mile. Since there are 60 minutes in a degree, one degree of latitude equals 60 NM everywhere on Earth.

q.t: Point A on the Earth's surface lies exactly on the parallel of latitude of 47°50'27''N. Which point is exactly 240 NM north of A?
q.e: 240 NM north equals 240 minutes of latitude. Dividing by 60 gives 4 degrees. 47° + 4° = 51°, so the new latitude is 51°50'27"N.

q.t: What is the distance between the two parallels of longitude 150°E and 151°E along the equator?
q.e: At the equator, the distance between degrees of longitude is at its maximum, where 1 minute of longitude equals 1 NM, making 1 degree equal to 60 NM.

q.t: What is the great circle distance between two points A and B on the equator when the difference between the two associated meridians is exactly one degree of longitude?
q.e: The equator itself is a great circle. One degree of arc along any great circle equals 60 minutes, which corresponds directly to 60 Nautical Miles.

q.t: Assume two arbitrary points A and B on the same parallel of latitude, but not on the equator. Point A is located on 010°E and point B on 020°E. The rumb line distance between A and B is always...
q.e: 10 degrees of longitude at the equator spans 600 NM. Since parallels of latitude shrink as they approach the poles, 10 degrees of longitude must span less than 600 NM anywhere off the equator.

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 20° of longitude?
q.e: The Earth rotates 15° per hour, which equates to 1° every 4 minutes. 20° * 4 minutes = 80 minutes, which is 1 hour and 20 minutes.

q.t: What is the difference in time when the sun moves 10° of longitude?
q.e: At a rotation rate of 1° every 4 minutes, 10 degrees of rotation takes exactly 40 minutes (0:40 h).

q.t: With Central European Summer Time (CEST) given as UTC+2, what UTC time corresponds to 1600 CEST?
q.e: To find UTC from CEST (UTC+2), you must subtract the 2-hour offset from the local time. 1600 - 2 hours = 1400 UTC.

q.t: UTC is...
o: a local time in Central Europe.
local mean time at a specific point on Earth.
an obligatory time used in aviation.
q.e: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is the primary time standard by which aviation regulates clocks globally to completely eliminate timezone confusion.

q.t: With Central European Time (CET) given as UTC+1, what UTC time corresponds to 1700 CET?
q.e: To convert CET (UTC+1) to UTC, subtract the 1-hour offset. 1700 - 1 hour = 1600 UTC.

q.t: Vienna (LOWW) is located at 016° 34'E, Salzburg (LOWS) at 013° 00'E. The latitude of both positions can be considered as equal. What is the difference of sunrise and sunset times, expressed in UTC, between Wien and Salzburg?
o: In Vienna the sunrise and sunset are about 4 minutes later than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise and sunset are about 14 minutes earlier than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise is 4 minutes later and sunset is 4 minutes earlier than in Salzburg
In Vienna the sunrise is 14 minutes earlier and sunset is 14 minutes later than in Salzburg
q.e: The difference in longitude is roughly 3.5 degrees. At 4 minutes per degree, 3.5 * 4 = 14 minutes. Because Vienna is further East, the sun rises and sets earlier there.

q.t: The term 'civil twilight' is defined as...
o: the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 12 degrees or less below the true horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 6 degrees or less below the apparent horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 6 degrees or less below the true horizon.
the period of time before sunrise or after sunset where the midpoint of the sun disk is 12 degrees or less below the apparent horizon.
q.e: Civil twilight begins or ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the true (ideal) horizon.

q.t: Given: TC: 179°; WCA: -12°; VAR: 004° E; DEV: +002° What are MH and MC?
q.e: True Heading (TH) = TC + WCA = 179 - 12 = 167°. Magnetic Heading (MH) = TH - VAR = 167 - 4 = 163°. Magnetic Course (MC) = TC - VAR = 179 - 4 = 175°.

q.t: The term ‚magnetic course' (MC) is defined as...
o: the angle between true north and the course line.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the magnetic north pole.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographic North Pole.
the angle between magnetic north and the course line.
q.e: Course refers to the intended path of the aircraft. Magnetic course is that intended path measured clockwise relative to magnetic north.

q.t: The term 'True Course' (TC) is defined as...
o: the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographic North Pole.
the angle between true north and the course line.
tthe angle between magnetic north and the course line.
the direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the magnetic north pole.
q.e: True Course is the intended path of the aircraft over the ground, measured clockwise starting from True (Geographic) North.

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200° What are TH and VAR?
q.e: True Heading (TH) = TC + WCA = 183 + 11 = 194°. Variation (VAR) = TH - MH = 194 - 198 = -4°, which translates to 4° West.

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200° What are the TH and the DEV?
q.e: True Heading (TH) = TC + WCA = 183 + 11 = 194°. Deviation (DEV) = MH - CH = 198 - 200 = -2°.

q.t: Given: TC: 183°; WCA: +011°; MH: 198°; CH: 200° What are the VAR and the DEV?
q.e: From previous derivations: TH = 194. VAR = TH - MH = 194 - 198 = -4 (4°W). DEV = MH - CH = 198 - 200 = -2 (-002°).

q.t: Where does the inclination reach its lowest value?
q.e: Magnetic inclination (dip) is the angle the magnetic field lines make with the surface. It is 0 degrees (its absolute lowest value) exactly at the magnetic equator.

q.t: The angle between compass north and magnetic north is called...
q.e: Deviation is the localized error induced by the aircraft's own metals and electronic fields, creating a discrepancy between Magnetic North and Compass North.

q.t: Which direction corresponds to 'compass north' (CN)?
o: The most northerly part of the magnetic compass in the aircraft, where the reading takes place
The direction from an arbitrary point on Earth to the geographical North Pole
The angle between the aircraft heading and magnetic north
The direction to which the direct reading compass aligns due to earth's and aircraft's magnetic fields
q.e: Compass North is the actual, uncorrected direction the needle points, influenced simultaneously by both the Earth's magnetic field and the aircraft's magnetic deviation.

q.t: The term 'isogonal' or 'isogonic line' is defined as a line on an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the same value of...
q.e: Isogonic lines connect points of equal magnetic variation on a chart, helping pilots convert between true and magnetic headings.

q.t: The term 'agonic line' is defined as a line on Earth or an aeronautical chart, connecting all points with the...
q.e: An agonic line is a specialized isogonic line connecting all points where the magnetic variation is exactly zero degrees (True North and Magnetic North align perfectly).

q.t: Which are the official basic units for horizontal distances used in aeronautical navigation and their abbreviations?
q.e: In standard ICAO aviation navigation, horizontal distances en route are almost exclusively measured in Nautical Miles (NM) and occasionally kilometers (km).

q.t: 1000 ft equal...
q.e: One foot is approximately 0.3048 meters. Therefore, 1000 feet is roughly equal to 304.8 meters, which rounds to 300 meters in general operational terms.

q.t: 5500 m equal...
q.e: 1 meter is roughly 3.28 feet. 5500 meters * 3.28 = 18,040 feet, heavily rounded to 18,000 ft (Flight Level 180).

q.t: Electronic devices on board of an aeroplane have influence on the...
q.e: Electronic devices and wiring generate electromagnetic fields that directly interfere with the magnetized needle in the direct reading compass, causing deviation errors.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Mercator chart?
o: The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as curved lines, rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines
The scales increases with latitude, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
The scale is constant, great circles are depicted as straight lines, rhumb lines are depicted as curved lines
q.e: On a Mercator projection, meridians are drawn parallel, meaning the scale distorts and increases massively near the poles. Rhumb lines are straight, while shortest paths (great circles) appear curved.

q.t: Which are the properties of a Lambert conformal chart?
o: The chart is conformal and nearly true to scale
Great circles are depicted as straight lines and the chart is an equal-area projection
Rhumb lines are depicted as straight lines and the chart is conformal
The chart is conformal and an equal-area projection
q.e: Lambert Conformal Conic charts preserve shapes and angles (conformal) and maintain a relatively constant scale across the primary charted area, making straight lines closely approximate great circles.

q.t: The distance between two airports is 220 NM. On an aeronautical navigation chart the pilot measures 40.7 cm for this distance. The chart scale is...
q.e: 220 NM = 220 * 1.852 km = 407.44 km. 407.44 km = 40,744,000 cm. Chart scale = Map distance / Actual distance = 40.7 / 40,744,000, which equals 1:1,000,000.

q.t: A distance of 7.5 cm on an aeronautical chart represents a distance of 60.745 NM in reality. What is the chart scale?
An aircraft travels 100 km in 56 minutes. The ground speed (GS) equals...
q.e: Speed = Distance / Time. 100 km / (56/60) hours = 100 * 60 / 56 = 107.14 km/h.

q.t: How many satellites are necessary for a precise and verified three-dimensional determination of the position?
q.e: A GPS receiver requires a minimum of 4 satellite signals to solve for 4 mathematical variables: latitude, longitude, altitude (3D position), and the receiver's clock error.

q.t: When using a GPS for tracking to the next waypoint, a deviation indication is shown by a vertical bar and dots to the left and to the right of the bar. What statement describes the correct interpretation of the display?
o: The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection is +-10 NM.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as angular distance in degrees; the scale for full deflection is +-10°.
The deviation of the bar from the center indicates the track error as absolute distance in NM; the scale for full deflection depends on the operating mode of the GPS.
q.e: Unlike a traditional VOR which shows angular deviation in degrees, a GPS Course Deviation Indicator (CDI) displays lateral cross-track error in absolute distance (NM). The scale sensitivity changes based on the flight mode (Enroute, Terminal, Approach).

q.t: What is meant by the term "terrestrial navigation"?
o: Orientation by instrument readings during visual flight
Orientation by ground features during visual flight
Orientation by GPS during visual flight
Orientation by ground celestial object during visual flight
q.e: Terrestrial navigation (often called pilotage) relies entirely on visually identifying physical ground landmarks and features to determine position and course.

q.t: What ground features should preferrably be used for orientation during visual flight?
q.e: Large, continuous, and highly visible linear features like major rivers, highways, and railroads make excellent "catching features" and tracking references from the air.

q.t: What should be considered regarding a scheduled flight over water, when land cannot be reached in case of an emergency landing?
o: Contact to the nearest ATC shall consist during the whole flight
The flight plan has to contain the exact waypoints
For all passengers there must be life jackets or lifeboats present
Transponder code 7600 has to be set during the whole flight
q.e: Safety regulations mandate that life jackets or flotation devices must be available for everyone on board when flying over water beyond safe gliding distance to the shore.

q.t: A wind shear is...
o: a meteorological downslope wind phenomenon in the alps.
a wind speed change of more than 15 kt.
a vertical or horizontal change of wind speed and wind direction.
a slow increase of the wind speed in altitudes above 13000 ft.
q.e: Wind shear is formally defined as a sudden and significant change in wind speed and/or wind direction over a short vertical or horizontal distance.

q.t: Which weather phenomenon is typically associated with wind shear?
q.e: Thunderstorms are notorious for producing severe wind shear due to violent, localized updrafts and sudden, powerful downdrafts (microbursts).

q.t: When do you expect wind shear?
o: During a summer day with calm winds
In calm wind in cold weather
q.e: Temperature inversions trap distinct layers of air, often allowing an upper layer to move at vastly different speeds and directions compared to the surface layer, creating significant wind shear at the boundary.

q.t: Wake turbulence is caused by...
o: wind shear at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
pressure compensation at the wingtip of an aerofoil.
jet blast behind a turbine engine.
turbulence at the downwind side of a mountain range.
q.e: Wake turbulence (wingtip vortices) forms because the high-pressure air beneath an aircraft's wing attempts to equalize with the low-pressure air above the wing by rolling up and over the wingtips.

q.t: Wake turbulence is particularly strong...
q.e: Wake turbulence is strongest when an aircraft is heavy, flying in a clean configuration, and flying at low speeds, as the high angle of attack creates the maximum pressure differential across the wings.

q.t: At temperature below 0 °C the pressure at the burner is at 0,2 MPa (2 bar). Is take-off permissable with the hot air balloon?
o: No, pressure at burner is too low
Yes, at low temperatures a low hull temperature is sufficient
q.e: A minimum fuel pressure (typically around 3 bar or higher) is required to generate a safe, effective, and stable burner flame. 2 bar indicates insufficient vapor pressure, making takeoff unsafe.

q.t: Before buildup, the buildup team has to be informed about correct behaviour at sudden critical situations how?
q.e: The pilot-in-command holds ultimate responsibility for the safety of the operation and must personally brief the ground crew on emergency and critical situation procedures before inflation begins.

q.t: A balloon pilot decides to use one or more separate gas containers for initial heating during buildup. To ensure a safe buildup ...
o: to expedite take-off, the gas containers have to be stored ouside.
the gas containers have to be fixed safely inside the basket.
no separate gas containers are allowed during buildup.
two gas containers (one inside, one outside) are to be used.
q.e: All gas cylinders used during the inflation process must be securely strapped and fixed inside the basket to prevent them from falling over, which could cause liquid propane to vent or create a serious fire hazard.

q.t: The stretch-out of the envelope of a hot-air balloon should be made:
o: To the lee side of the basket
To the luv side of the basket
To the sunward side of the basket
To the sun-averted side of the basket
q.e: The envelope should be laid out downwind (on the lee side) of the basket. This allows the wind to help keep the fabric clear of the burner flame and assists in smoothly inflating the envelope as hot air rises into it.

q.t: During buildup of a hot-air balloon, who has to be equipped with tight, flame resistant gloves and clothing covering all body parts?
o: balloon pilot, buildup team and spectators
the balloon pilot and the buildup team
q.e: Both the pilot operating the burner and the crew members handling the lines and holding the envelope mouth must wear appropriate protective clothing (long sleeves, natural fibers, leather gloves) to prevent burns.

q.t: What has to be expected during descent above a heated water surface?
q.e: A heated water surface warms the air immediately above it. When a descending balloon enters this warmer (less dense) air, the temperature differential between the inside and outside of the balloon shrinks, reducing buoyancy and accelerating the sink rate.

q.t: What has to be considered before a balloon ride across water surfaces?
o: Continuous radio communication has to be established with air traffice control
A transponder has to be installed and carried aboard
A flight plan with detailled routing has to be filed.
For all people inside the basket life jackets have to be carried aboard
q.e: Aviation safety regulations strictly mandate that if a flight over water is planned and a safe glide to land is impossible, every person on board must be provided with a life jacket.

q.t: What has to be considered at moderate wind speeds during a balloon ride across mountainous area with cloud-free sky?
o: Lee waves and severe up- and downdrafts
q.e: Wind flowing over mountain ridges creates standing waves (lee waves) on the downwind side. These generate severe, invisible updrafts and downdrafts that can easily overpower a balloon's climb or descent capabilities.

q.t: During a balloon ride, visibility continiously becomes poorer, also cloud base decreases in direction of the current track. How should the balloon pilot react to this situation?
o: Use GPS or radio navigation to continue ride in clouds
Use next best chance for landing
Break through the clouds and continue above clouds
q.e: Balloons operate strictly under Visual Flight Rules (VFR). If weather conditions deteriorate toward Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC), the pilot is required to land as soon as a safe opportunity presents itself.

q.t: Under which conditions, no harzards should be expected for a balloon ride?
o: With high pressure areas before sunset
q.e: High pressure areas typically bring stable, calm, and clear weather. In the late afternoon before sunset, thermal activity ceases, creating the smoothest and most predictable flying conditions for balloons.

q.t: What wind conditions should be expected in the vicinity of showers or thunderstorms?
o: Steady wind from direction of shower.
Steady wind into direction of shower.
Calm winds during passage of a shower.
q.e: Showers and thunderstorms generate powerful, cold downdrafts that hit the ground and spread out rapidly and unpredictably, causing sudden, violent gust fronts from highly variable directions.

q.t: How may passengers assist the balloon pilot during landing preparation?
q.e: Passengers should help by securing all loose items (cameras, bags, bottles) so they do not become dangerous projectiles upon landing impact. Only the pilot is permitted to operate the balloon's flight controls.

q.t: What are primary criteria for selecting a landing site? 1. Obstacle situation 2. Elevation of the site 3. Strength of surface wind
q.e: The presence of obstacles (such as power lines and trees) and the strength of the surface wind are the two most critical safety factors when choosing where to land. The elevation of the site is less critical than avoiding direct physical hazards.

q.t: Which wind system may be dangerous for balloon rides in the Alps?
q.e: Foehn winds are strong, dry, and gusty downslope winds on the lee side of the Alps. They are associated with severe mechanical turbulence and rotor clouds, making them extremely dangerous for ballooning.

q.t: What has to be considered before touchdown of a hot-air balloon during landing?
o: Cut off gas feed to the ignition flames.
q.e: Shutting off the pilot lights (ignition flames) and the main gas supply before ground impact is a critical safety step to prevent a fire in case a fuel line ruptures or the basket tips over.

q.t: On summerdays with calm winds, the balloon pilot has to expect:
o: With a cold air pool on the ground.
q.e: Intense solar radiation heats the ground, which in turn heats the lowest layers of air. This generates strong thermal updrafts (convection) which can unpredictably affect the balloon's altitude and control.

q.t: What has to be done in case the balloon shows a strong tendency to climb while crossing thermals?
o: It must be heated continuously to maintain hull temperature.
It must be heated stronger than usual.
The burner has to be cut off immediately.
The pull-rope has to be actuated immediately.
q.e: A thermal carries the balloon upward. If the pilot stops heating, the air inside the envelope will cool down. When the balloon eventually exits the thermal, it will lack the required buoyancy and drop uncontrollably. Maintaining internal temperature is vital.

q.t: What has to be expected by the balloon pilot during descent in deeply cooled layers close to the ground?
o: Increasing descent while entering to ground layers
Floating on top of the cold air layer.
q.e: Cold air pooling near the ground in an inversion is significantly denser than the air above it. As the balloon descends into this denser air, it gains relative buoyancy and tends to 'bounce' or float on top of the cold layer, requiring venting to break through.

q.t: In case of a water landing, when should the life jackets be inflated?
o: After landing, still in the basket, if leaving the basket has to be expected.
q.e: Life jackets should only be inflated AFTER exiting the basket. Inflating them while still inside the basket can cause occupants to become trapped if the basket flips over, sinks, or gets entangled with ropes.

q.t: Why has a secondary ingnition source be available during a ride with a hot-air balloon?
o: As an emergency lighting during night.
To check seals of hose connections during darkness.
To provide light signals by a camping fire after an emergency landing.
To re-ingnite the burner or pilot flames after flameout.
q.e: If the primary pilot light accidentally goes out (flameout), an independent, secondary ignition source (like a striker or flint lighter) is absolutely vital to relight the burner and maintain altitude control.

q.t: What is the consequence if the pressure at the burner valve is lower than 0.28 MPa (lower than 2.8 bar)?
o: Tha gas container should be heated by the flame.
The heating system may be damaged.
The pressure in the gas container may be increased by use of acetylene.
q.e: Below a minimum safe operating pressure (typically around 2.8 bar), the burner cannot produce a flame powerful enough to safely launch, arrest a descent, or maneuver the balloon. Therefore, take-off is strictly prohibited.

q.t: What action has to be considered by the pilot of a hot-air balloon with a double-burner installation, in case one burner valve fails?
o: An emergency call should be made.
Both burner valves have to be shut down immediately.
The ride has to be stopped immediately.
The ride can be continued by use of the remaining burner.
q.e: A double-burner system provides mechanical redundancy. If one burner fails, the pilot can safely isolate the faulty side and continue operating the balloon using the fully functional independent second burner to execute a safe landing.

q.t: At high altitude, the complete heating system of a hot-air balloon fails. What maximum rate of descent has to be expected upon reaching ground?
q.e: If a hot air balloon cools entirely, the envelope acts essentially as a parachute. The terminal sink rate of a standard balloon envelope is approximately 6.5 m/s (roughly 1300 ft/min), which will result in a hard but survivable impact.

q.t: What may be the consequence, if gas containers of a hot-air balloon are refilled at temperatures below 0 °C by volume (80%)?
o: Too low pressure at high temperatures.
Less burner power at high temperatures.
